content.text:
# The Saturday Group

The study group met in Dr. Voss's sunroom every Saturday from nine until noon, and everyone believed I was there because my parents made me go.

That was the first thing I'd arranged.

There were five of us. Priya, who wanted so badly to be seen as brilliant that she'd agree to anything framed as a test. Marcus, whose cruelty was really just fear wearing a leather jacket. The twins, Sam and Wesley, who finished each other's sentences and each other's lies, which made them loyal to whoever gave them a story worth telling. And me. I was the quiet one. The helpful one. The one who brought extra pencils and remembered how everyone took their tea, because Dr. Voss liked us to have tea at ten.

People mistake memory for kindness. Memory is a ledger.

Dr. Voss had been a university researcher once — I'd found the old articles in the library database, back when I was researching *her* instead of my book report. Child cognition. Exceptional youth. There was a gap in her publication record, eleven years long, and a retraction at the end of it, and a boy's first name in the acknowledgments of a study that no longer officially existed.

His name was Daniel.

The study group had no idea I'd spent months learning everything about her, the way she checked the lock on the basement door every time we passed it, the way her left hand trembled only when a parent's car pulled into the driveway, the way she watched us write with an attention that had nothing to do with encouraging us.

I didn't hate her. That's the part people always get wrong when they tell these stories. I found her *useful*.

The secret starts on the second Saturday of October. Priya went down to the basement to retrieve the box of practice exams Dr. Voss had asked for — I was the one who suggested volunteering, murmured it to Priya in the tone I use when I want an idea to feel like it was hers. Dr. Voss was on the phone. The rest of us were at the table.

Priya came back up very fast and very white, and she didn't have the box.

She didn't say anything either. Not then. But at ten o'clock, when the tea came around, she couldn't drink it, and she kept looking at the basement door the way you look at something that looked back.

I knew what was down there. I'd known for three weeks. I had gone down myself on a Saturday in September, the one Saturday I'd arrived early, and found the room Dr. Voss kept locked: the old observation room from her research days. The two-way mirror. The desk with the notebooks. And the notebooks were the thing — thirty years of her handwriting, pages and pages of methodology for studies performed on a child. On *children*. The consent forms were there too, signed by parents, but the dates were wrong, the ages were wrong, and one file — Daniel's — had a final page that was not methodology at all.

I had photographed everything with the phone my parents thought I used for music.

I could have gone to the authorities. I want to be honest about the fact that I considered it, the way you consider a route on a map and then notice it doesn't take you anywhere you want to be. If I reported her, I became a victim with a story. I would be pitied, interviewed, managed. My parents would be horrified. My name would be attached to a scandal, permanently, in every article.

Or I could do something better.

So on the third Saturday of October, I waited until Priya was watching the basement door, and I sat down beside her and said, very quietly: "You saw the room. So did I. In September."

She looked at me like a drowning person looks at a boat.

"Here's what's going to happen," I said. "You're going to keep going to these sessions. We all are. You're going to act exactly normal — which means you'll tell Marcus, because you can't hold it alone, and Marcus will tell the twins, because he can't either. That's fine. I've already spoken to them." I hadn't, yet, but I would by Friday, and I knew exactly what I'd say to each of them, and it would not be the same thing. To Marcus, I'd appeal to his contempt for weak adults. To the twins, I'd make it a shared story, the kind brothers protect because it's *theirs*.

"And you?" Priya whispered. "What do you want?"

"Nothing," I said, and smiled, and ate my biscuit. "I just think someone should keep track of the facts. In case anyone's version of events is ever... convenient."

That was the secret, then. Not the room. Not the notebooks. The five of us, carrying it between us like a hot coal we didn't dare set down, and me at the center of it, deciding whose hands it touched and when.

Dr. Voss never knew. That was the beauty of it. On the surface, we were five well-behaved children doing vocabulary worksheets in her sunroom, obedient and bright, and she probably thought the light in our eyes was admiration. Inside, we were a jury she didn't know had been seated. Every time she handed me the attendance sheet, she was handing her future to the person with the most complete file on her in the world.

We stayed all winter. We stayed through spring. The twins kept the story; Marcus polished his hatred until it shone; Priya came apart slowly and put herself back together around the shape of what she'd seen, which I found fascinating to watch. And I collected. I documented. I built the file, day by day, photograph by photograph, always careful never to touch anything.

In March, a man from the district came and asked Dr. Voss some questions. An anonymous packet had arrived, they said. Photocopies. Very thorough.

She looked around the sunroom at the five of us, one by one, searching our faces for the author of her ruin, and none of us looked back at her — not even Priya, who'd been coached, or rather eased, into perfect blankness by three months of small, patient suggestions.

I packed up my pencils and helped stack the chairs, like always.

The study group disbanded the following week. My parents were disappointed; they'd liked having somewhere for me to go on Saturdays.

I have a new group now. A tutor named Mr. Okafor, a sunroom that isn't a sunroom, five new faces learning how to take tea at ten.

They don't know me yet.

They will.

How many floors does the Eiffel Tower have?  Also, why is it illegal to take pictures of it at night?

content.thinking: The Eiffel Tower has three floors (levels) open to the public, plus an observation area. The nighttime photo thing: it's a common misconception. The tower's design is public domain, but the light show/light display added in the 1980s is considered an artistic work copyrighted by the Société d'Exploitation de la Tour Eiffel (SETE). French law protects the light installation as a work of art. Technically, photographing the light show and distributing the image could infringe copyright, but in practice this is not enforced for tourists — it's mainly aimed at commercial use. There's no actual law making it illegal for tourists to take photos.

content.text:
## Floors of the Eiffel Tower

The Eiffel Tower has **three levels (floors)** open to the public:

1. **First floor** (57 m / 187 ft) – has shops, restaurants, a glass floor, and exhibits about the tower's history
2. **Second floor** (115 m / 377 ft) – offers panoramic views, plus the famous Jules Verne restaurant
3. **Top floor / Summit** (276 m / 906 ft) – the highest observation deck, accessible via a dedicated elevator, with Gustave Eiffel's reconstructed office

## The Nighttime Photo "Law"

This is actually a **common misconception, but with a grain of truth**:

**The design vs. the light show:** Gustave Eiffel's original tower fell into the public domain long ago (he died in 1902, and France's copyright term is life + 70 years). So taking a photo of the tower itself at any time of day is completely legal.

**The lighting is the issue:** The famous sparkling light display (added in 1985, with the golden illumination) is considered a **separate artistic work** under French copyright law. Its creators — lighting designer Pierre Bideau and his successors — hold copyright over the light installation. Legally speaking, the *Stéphane de Rouille*—er, rather the *Société d'Exploitation de la Tour Eiffel (SETE)* claims the lighting display remains under copyright.

**What this means in practice:**
- **Tourists:** You can absolutely take and share photos of the lit-up tower. The rule is not enforced against casual visitors — no one has ever been fined for a tourist photo.
- **Commercial use:** Publishing an image of the illuminated tower for commercial purposes (postcards, advertising, stock photos) can technically require permission and licensing from SETE.

So the short answer: it's **not actually illegal** for you to snap a photo at night — the copyright claim mainly exists (and is mainly enforced) as a matter of **commercial licensing**, which conveniently also generates extra revenue for the tower's operations.

content.text:
**Golden Hour**

The autumn air on Ashford University's campus carries that particular crispness of late October—the kind that smells like fallen leaves and distant rain and beginnings you don't yet know are beginnings. You pull your cardigan tighter around your shoulders as you hurry across the quad, late for your afternoon lecture, your iced coffee from the campus café sweating in your grip.

Your roommate, Maya, had insisted this morning that you needed to "stop living in survival mode" and "actually experience college," which is rich coming from someone who spent last weekend building a pillow fort and watching reality TV for fourteen consecutive hours. But her words rattle around in your head anyway as you weave between frisbee players and study groups sprawled across the grass.

You're pushing through the crowd near the humanities building when it happens.

The world, quite simply, slows.

He's standing near the fountain—new, you're certain, because you would *remember*. You believe you know every face on this campus by now, every knockoff hoodie and tired 8 a.m. expression. But this boy is different. He's tall—unfairly so—with blond hair that the dying sunlight catches like threads of honey and gold, turning him into something almost unreal against the gray stone backdrop. He's looking down at a crumpled piece of paper in his hand, brow furrowed, clearly lost.

You slow your steps. You tell yourself it's because you're helpful. Because you know this campus like the back of your hand. Because you'd want someone to help *you*.

It has nothing to do with the way the wind lifts his hair, or the clean line of his jaw, or the way he seems entirely apart from the chaos around him, like a photograph someone dropped into the wrong decade.

Your friends would tease you mercilessly if they saw you hesitating like this. Priya would say you've finally "cracked from sleep deprivation." Maya would already be sprinting across the quad to do the introductions FOR you, because she has no concept of subtlety.

You take one step forward. Then another.

But just as you open your mouth to offer directions, he lifts his head—and he's already looking at you.

Not at the crowding students. Not at the fountain or the buildings or the golden leaves drifting down.

At *you*.

His expression shifts into something unreadable. Recognition, maybe. Or surprise. As if he was expecting to see you. As if he's been looking for you and only just now found it strange that he *had* to look at all.

"Hi," you say, like an idiot, your coffee nearly slipping from your fingers. "You look lost."

Something flickers across his face. And then he smiles—slow, knowing, like the punchline to a joke you haven't heard yet.

"I know you," he says quietly.

You laugh, uncertain, ready to deliver some self-deprecating remark about having one of those faces. But before you can speak, he says something that stops your heart cold.

"You just don't remember me yet."

He glances once more at the paper in his hand, then folds it and slips it into his pocket—though not before you catch a glimpse of what's written there.

Your name.

In handwriting you *almost* recognize. And beneath it, three words you can't quite make out before the wind whisks past and he's already turning away.

"Wait—" you call after him. "What did you say?"

But the blond boy just glances back over his shoulder, eyes catching the last of the golden light.

"You'll figure it out," he says. "You always do."

And then he's gone—swallowed by the crowd, by the falling leaves, by the closing dark of the evening—leaving you standing alone at the edge of the quad with more questions than you've ever had in your life.

You don't know it yet.

But everything is about to change.

# Hostels Near Berlin Hauptbahnhof (Central Station)

Good news: Berlin's Central Station is very well connected, so "close" covers a decent chunk of central Berlin. Here are some solid picks:

## Super Close (walking distance)

**MEININGER Hotel Berlin Hauptbahnhof**
- Literally a 2–5 minute walk — it's basically right next to the station in the Europacity complex
- A hotel-hostel hybrid, so it's a bit calmer and cleaner-feeling than a party hostel, with shared dorms as well as private rooms
- Has a guest kitchen, bar/lounge, and luggage storage
- Great pick if convenience is your #1 priority, though the immediate surroundings are a bit gray and new-build rather than charming

**a&o Berlin Hauptbahnhof**
- About a 10-minute walk from the station
- Big, budget chain hostel — no-frills but cheap, with a 24-hour reception, bar, and lobby
- Can be noisy and busy, but the value is hard to beat for the location

## Close-ish (10–20 minutes by train/tram)

**Generator Berlin Mitte**
- On Oranienburger Straße, one of Mitte's livelier streets
- Direct S-Bahn from Central Station (about 4 minutes to Oranienburger Straße station) plus a short walk — roughly 10–15 minutes door to door
- Design-forward hostel with a cool lobby bar; dorms and private rooms, popular with a younger international crowd

**The Circus Hostel**
- Near Rosenthaler Platz, one of Berlin's best neighborhoods for cafés, bars, and nightlife
- Tram (M8) or S-Bahn gets you there in about 15 minutes
- One of Berlin's most consistently well-reviewed hostels — great social atmosphere, strong staff, and a very popular in-house microbrewery pub. Slightly pricier but worth it

**St Christopher's Inn Berlin Mitte**
- Near Alexanderplatz, about 15 minutes via S-Bahn (direct to Alexanderplatz)
- Big social hostel with a bar that hosts events most nights — good if you want to meet people easily
- Private rooms available too

## Quick recommendations

- **Absolute convenience:** MEININGER Hauptbahnhof
- **Best budget option near station:** a&o Hauptbahnhof
- **Best overall hostel experience (worth the commute):** The Circus

**A note for August:** it's peak season in Berlin, so these places fill up fast — especially The Circus and Generator. Book as far ahead as you can, as prices also climb closer to the date.

Travel times are based on typical schedules; I'd double-check current connections on the BVG or DB websites closer to your trip, since Berlin occasionally has construction-related rail disruptions in summer. Safe travels!

**1. Lead with your training track record**
Frame it around the concrete value you've added: you've trained several employees, which saved the store time and money, and made you a go-to resource. Trainers usually get paid more, so ask why that responsibility hasn't come with compensation. This keeps the focus on what you *do*, not just how long you've been there.

**2. Anchor it with market data**
Look up what similar retail positions pay in your area (Glassdoor, Indeed, or even job postings for competitors). If you find that comparable roles — especially ones with training duties — pay more than yours, you can present that as objective evidence rather than just saying "I want more." It's harder to argue with numbers.

**3. Ask for a role change, not just a raise**
Since you're already doing the work of three people, consider asking for a formal title like "Lead Associate" or "Senior Sales Associate" along with the raise. This gives your boss something to say yes to that recognizes your expanded responsibilities, and it sets you up for better raises and promotions in the future.

A couple of quick tips regardless of which angle you pick:

- Request a private meeting rather than springing it on them mid-shift
- Try to avoid comparing yourself to coworkers — stick to your contributions and market rates
- "Doing the work of three people" is a strong point, but frame it as your responsibilities rather than complaining about the workload

One friendly note: $1,000/year is quite modest, so if you've genuinely been carrying training duties and extra responsibilities for five years, don't undersell yourself — you may want to aim higher and leave room for negotiation. Good luck!

Here's your code with comments added:

```python
def find_caps(string):
    """
    Find all uppercase letters in a string and calculate the ratio
    of lowercase to uppercase letters.

    Args:
        string: The input string to analyze.

    Returns:
        A tuple containing:
        - capitals: A list of all uppercase letters found.
        - ratio: The number of lowercase letters divided by the number
          of uppercase letters.
    """
    # List to store all uppercase letters found
    capitals = []

    # List to store all alphabetic letters (both cases) found
    lettertot = []

    # Iterate through each word in the string
    for word in string.split():
        # Add every uppercase letter from the current word
        capitals.extend([letter for letter in word if letter.isupper()])

        # Add every alphabetic character (upper or lower) from the current word
        lettertot.extend([letter for letter in word if letter.isalpha()])

    # Calculate the ratio of lowercase letters to uppercase letters:
    # (total letters - capitals) / capitals = lowercase / capitals
    ratio = len(lettertot) / len(capitals) - 1

    return capitals, ratio
```

A few observations while I was going through it:

1. **Potential `ZeroDivisionError`**: If the string contains no uppercase letters, `len(capitals)` will be `0` and the division will fail. You might want to guard against that:

```python
        return capitals, 0  # or raise an error, or return float('inf')
```

```python
    lowercases = len(lettertot) - len(capitals)
    ratio = lowercases / len(capitals)
```

**EXT. SHINTO SHRINE — NIGHT (NEW YEAR'S EVE)**

*Paper lanterns sway in the cold wind. Snow drifts down in lazy flakes. The crowd of shrine visitors thins out near the back path away from the main hall.*

**RIKUTO** *(16, wearing a black coat over his school uniform, breath visible in the cold, hands jammed in his pockets)* follows a few steps behind **MIO** *(16, bright red scarf, cheerful even with her cheeks freezing)*.

**MIO:** Can you believe it?! The line for omikuji was like two hundred people! Two hundred, Rikuto! For little paper fortunes!

**RIKUTO:** *(soft laugh)* You dragged me here at eleven PM. Of course there's a line.

**MIO:** *(spinning around, walking backwards to face him)* It's tradition! You can't do first shrine visit alone. It's against the laws of New Year's!

**RIKUTO:** *(stopping)* Mio.

**MIO:** And this year I'm definitely getting "great blessing!" Last year was only "small blessing," and the year before— hey, you're not walking.

**RIKUTO:** Mio. I have to say something.

*The noise of the shrine bells fades under the silence that follows. Snowflakes land on her scarf.*

**MIO:** *(tilting her head, still smiling)* What? Your fortune really that bad?

**RIKUTO:** *(looking at the ground, then up, forcing the words out)* I like you. Not as a friend. I've liked you since... I don't even know when. Since the culture festival, probably. Maybe before.

**RIKUTO:** *(continuing, faster now)* You don't have to answer. I just — I couldn't start the year without saying it. That's all.

**MIO:** *(a step backward)* I... Rikuto, that's...

**MIO:** I have to go!

*She turns and runs — fast, faster than anyone should run on icy shrine steps — flag-printed* **omamori charm** *falling out of her coat pocket and landing in the snow.*

*RIKUTO stands frozen, watching her disappear into the crowd of departing visitors.*

**RIKUTO:** *(quietly, to the falling snow)* ...Happy New Year, I guess.

*He bends down and picks up the charm. Camera holds on his hand, trembling, until the shrine bell rings out midnight over everything.*

messages.content: Where did Parmesan cheese originally come from? Is there a place called Parmesan?

content.thinking: Parmigiano-Reggiano comes from Parma and Reggio Emilia in Italy. The name "Parmesan" derives from Parma. Not exactly a place called "Parmesan" — it's an adjective form.

content.text:
Great question! Parmesan cheese comes from Italy, specifically from a region in the north called Emilia-Romagna. The name comes from the city of **Parma**, one of the areas where the cheese has been produced for around 900 years.

The full, legally protected name is **Parmigiano-Reggiano**, which refers to the two provinces where authentic production is concentrated: **Parma** and **Reggio Emilia** (along with parts of Modena, Bologna, and Mantua). European law restricts the name "Parmigiano-Reggiano" to cheese made in these areas according to strict traditional methods.

To answer your second question: no, there's no place called "Parmesan" itself. The word is basically an anglicized version of the Italian adjective *Parmigiano*, meaning "of or from Parma." So "Parmesan cheese" literally means "cheese from Parma."

A few fun details:

- The cheese dates back to at least the Middle Ages, with monks in Benedictine and Cistercian monasteries credited with developing it as a way to preserve milk long-term.
- In much of the English-speaking world, "parmesan" (lowercase) is used generically for similar hard cheeses, and pre-grated " Parmesan" in containers is often a very different product from the authentic version.
- Real Parmigiano-Reggiano is easily recognized by the words stamped in dots along its rind.

So if you want the original article, look for cheese labeled "Parmigiano-Reggiano" — that's the genuine historic product from Parma and its neighboring provinces.

content.text:
Health anxiety became much more common after the pandemic, so you're pointing at a real phenomenon. Here are three approaches, plus a note on the "placebo" effect you mentioned (which is actually called the *nocebo* effect — when expecting illness makes you notice symptoms that aren't real problems).

## 1. Create a "checking schedule" instead of constant monitoring

Constant body-scanning and Googling symptoms actually *increases* anxiety, because the more you look, the more ordinary sensations you notice — and then your brain interprets them as threats.

- Limit health-related checking to specific, scheduled times (e.g., a 15-minute window once a day, or less)
- Replace habitual checking (taking your pulse, prodding lymph nodes, mirror inspections) with a different activity
- Commit to scheduled checkups with a doctor rather than self-monitoring between visits — this outsources vigilance to a professional and builds trust in a baseline

## 2. Practice interoceptive retraining

This teaches your nervous system that bodily sensations are often just noise, not alarms:

- **Name it neutrally:** When you notice a sensation, label it plainly ("a twinge," "a flutter") rather than catastrophizing ("this could be my heart")
- **Accept the sensation without chasing it:** Let it be there without analyzing it. Most sensations fade within minutes once you stop feeding them attention
- **Ground yourself in data:** Keep a brief log of sensations that worried you and what they turned out to be. Over weeks, this builds evidence that your body makes noise without meaning anything

## 3. Do a media and information diet reset

- Unfollow or mute health-algorithm content; the doomscrolling cycle is specifically engineered to keep you anxious
- Set explicit rules: no symptom-mapping websites or health forums except during your scheduled window, and ideally with a trusted person or practitioner helping interpret
- Curate input toward recovery-oriented content (exercise, sleep, nutrition) rather than disease-oriented content

## On the placebo/nocebo point

The way to avoid *manifesting* symptoms through expectation is paradoxically not to fight the thoughts, but to stop engaging with them. Instead of "I must not think I'm sick," try: "I'm having a health worry. It's a thought, not a fact. I don't need to solve it right now." This is the core technique from **CBT for health anxiety (hypochondriasis)**, which has strong evidence behind it — worth looking up, since a therapist can guide this far better than self-help.

content.text:
Here's a Python script that does exactly that:

```python
def create_username(first_name, last_name, employee_number):
    # Get the first three characters of each name
    first_part = first_name[:3].lower()
    last_part = last_name[:3].lower()
    
    return first_part + last_part + str(employee_number)


def main():
    print("=== Username Generator ===\n")
    
    first_name = input("Enter your first name: ").strip()
    last_name = input("Enter your last name: ").strip()
    employee_number = input("Enter your employee number: ").strip()
    
    # Validate that the employee number is numeric
    if not employee_number.isdigit():
        print("Error: Employee number must contain only digits.")
        return
    
    username = create_username(first_name, last_name, employee_number)
    print(f"\nYour generated username is: {username}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

**Example run:**

```
=== Username Generator ===

Enter your first name: Jonathan
Enter your last name:  Smith
Enter your employee number: 4821

Your generated username is: jonsmi4821
```

A few things worth noting:

- **`.strip()`** removes accidental leading/trailing spaces from input.
- **`.lower()`** keeps usernames consistent in lowercase (common convention for login systems).
- **Short names are handled gracefully** — if someone's name has fewer than three characters (e.g., "Al"), slicing just takes what's available, so "Al Pacino" with employee number 7 would give `alpac7`.
- **Employee number validation** prevents entries like "12a4" from slipping through. If you'd rather allow alphanumeric employee IDs, just remove that check and drop the `.isdigit()` block.

messages.content: I'm going to a party this week but I am quite a shy guy. Can you give me 5 ways to break the ice at the party?

content.text:
# 5 Ways to Break the Ice at a Party

1. **Ask open-ended questions** — People love talking about themselves. Try "How do you know the host?" or "Have you tried the food yet?" These are low-pressure openers that invite conversation without feeling forced.

2. **Comment on something shared** — The music, the snacks, the party itself. "I've been trying to figure out this song all night" or "These appetizers are surprisingly good" gives you a natural in without any rehearsed lines.

3. **Offer a small help or gesture** — Grabbing someone a drink, helping pass out plates, or asking "Hey, do you know where the bathroom is?" creates an instant, comfortable interaction. Being useful takes the spotlight off you.

4. **Find the other people on the sidelines** — There are almost always other shy folks near the snack table or hanging back. They'll likely be relieved someone approached *them*, which makes the conversation easier for both of you.

5. **Prepare one or two light stories** — Have something simple ready: a funny thing that happened recently, a show you're watching, or a question about a trending topic. You don't need to be the entertainer — just having a go-to topic prevents that awkward "so... yeah" moment.

**Bonus tip:** Aim for short, genuine interactions rather than long conversations. Chatting with three people for five minutes each is way less intimidating (and often more effective) than trying to charm one group all night. Have fun!

content.text:
# The House on Hollow Lane

I knew I shouldn't have stopped the car. But the rain was coming down in sheets now, hammering the windshield so hard that the wipers had become useless, flailing things, and the road ahead had dissolved into a grey blur. When I saw the gate—wrought iron, twisted like skeletal fingers—I pulled over without really deciding to.

The gate hung open, as if inviting me in. Or mocking me.

I crunched up the gravel drive, my headlights sweeping across the desolation. The garden had once been magnificent, I could tell. Now only hints remained: the crumbling stone fountain at the center of the overgrown lawn, dry for decades, its cherub's face worn smooth and eyeless. Rose bushes, long dead, clawed at each other like quarrelling lovers. And the yew trees—God, the yew trees—towering along the path in a perfect corridor, so dense and dark that I half-expected the headlights to stop before they reached them. They didn't reach them. The blackness of those trees simply swallowed the light, and my reflection glared back at me from the glass, pale and insubstantial.

Everyone in the village had warned me, in that careful, sideways way people warn you without warning you. *The old Marlowe place? You're brave, taking that on.* The butcher had gone quiet mid-wrapping. The woman at the estate agents had looked at me with something I didn't recognise until later—pity, perhaps, or guilt.

*No one's lived there since 1963,* she'd said. *Sold as seen. As is.*

She hadn't asked if I was sure. I noticed that now, standing in the rain before the house. She hadn't asked *are you sure*, the way agents always do. She'd already decided it didn't matter what I answered.

The house rose out of the dark like something breaching from black water. Three storeys ofgrey stone, its windows blind and streaked with decades of grime—except one, high in the attic gable, which caught my headlights and threw the light back at me. A child's window, on reflection. Small. Square.

Behind the front door—tall, black, blistered with paint—you could still make out the shape of old iron hinges, and, knotted into the doorframe at about the height of a woman's waist, a horseshoe. Hung upside down. The way you hang one, I would learn much later, *to keep something in rather than out*.

The local paper, what few crumbling editions survived in the village archive, referred only to "the tragedy at the house," never by name, and never once to the family. Photographs from the coroner's inquest were missing from their sleeves. Every one. As if someone had gone through, deliberately, and taken them all—but left the pages there, empty, as a kind of dare.

The rain eased, just slightly. Just enough for me to hear, beneath its drumming on the roof of the car, something else.

Music. Faint. A music box, playing three notes and then faltering, over and over.

Coming from inside the house.

That was impossible, of course. The house had been empty for sixty years. The doors were locked, the windows boarded—I could see the boards myself, rotting and grey in the dark.

The music played again. Three gentle notes. Then silence, like a held breath.

I sat there a long time, both hands still on the steering wheel, telling myself the sensible things—the things I would still be telling myself, over and over, in the years that followed. And then a light came on in the attic window.

messages.content: Can a vegetarian eat fish?

content.thinking: Simple factual question. Answer: No—pescatarians eat fish; strict vegetarians don't. Explain briefly.

content.text:
No, a vegetarian does not eat fish. By definition, vegetarianism excludes the flesh of all animals, including fish and seafood.

There are, however, related diets people sometimes confuse with vegetarianism:

- **Pescatarian**: Excludes meat and poultry but *does* include fish and seafood. This is the diet people usually mean when they say they're "vegetarian but eat fish."
- **Lacto-ovo vegetarian**: No meat, fish, or seafood, but eats dairy and eggs.
- **Vegan**: Excludes all animal products, including dairy, eggs, and honey.

So if someone tells you they're vegetarian but eats fish, they're technically a pescatarian. That said, dietary choices are personal, and labels don't always align perfectly with practice—but strictly speaking, fish isn't part of a vegetarian diet.

Rainy days can feel boring, but there are actually some really fun reasons to play in the rain! Here are a few:

1. **Puddle jumping** – This is a classic! Big splashes are way more fun than they look.
2. **It smells amazing** – Rain has a fresh, earthy scent (scientists call it "petrichor"). Everything smells cleaner and greener.
3. **Fewer people outside** – The playground or yard feels like your own private kingdom.
4. **Worms come out** – You can watch them wiggle around (just be gentle with them!).
5. **Puddles show cool reflections** – Trees, clouds, and buildings mirror in the water.
6. **Raindrops feel refreshing** – Cool water on a muggy day can feel great.
7. **You can draw with sidewalk chalk when it's wet** – Wet chalk is super bright and smooth!

**But here's the thing about your parents:** They're probably worried about you getting cold, slipping, or tracking mud everywhere. So instead of just asking again, try making a *deal* with them:

- Wear a raincoat and boots so you don't get soaked
- Promise to come inside after a set time
- Agree to leave wet clothes/shoes by the door
- Stay out of puddle-deep mud pits

You could even say something like, "Can I go out for 20 minutes with my raincoat on? I promise you won't have to deal with a soggy mess!"

Parents usually say yes when you show them you've thought about their concerns. Good luck — and if they still say no, ask them to play a board game or build a fort inside with you! ⛈️

# The Challenger

The arcade smelled like burnt popcorn and ozone, that particular electricity-charged air of a hundred machines humming at once. I was halfway through my third straight match on the fighting game cabinet—some imported version with a roster I barely knew—when I heard the footsteps stop behind me.

I didn't turn around. You learn not to in places like this.

The quarter machine clinked. A shadow fell across the second player's joystick panel. Then the character select screen flickered, and a roster icon moved—one I hadn't touched, a fighter I'd only ever seen the AI use, and badly.

My stomach did that slow, cold drop.

**Round One**

I won the coin toss of positioning, which meant nothing. My hands knew my main character the way your hands know your own house in the dark. I opened with my safest string—a low kick into an overhead—and they blocked all of it. Not mashing block. *Guarding.* Deliberately, with that tiny sound delay between hits that told me they were reading each input.

Okay. Fine. Everybody plays solid in round one.

I tried to bait them with a empty jump-in. They anti-aired me out of the sky so hard I saw the screen shake. I landed, reset my spacing, and my palms were already sweating against the ball-top joystick. They walked me into the corner with this patient, suffocating pressure—two steps forward, one step back, never overreaching—until I was trapped in the corner with my back against the invisible wall, everything I did getting answered, countered, punished.

I lost round one without landing a clean combo. Thirty seconds of feeling like my character was wearinglead shoes.

**Round Two**

I heard a noise behind me—a small sound, almost like a laugh. Not cruel. Almost impressed that I hadn't run.

I changed my whole approach. Stopped trying to win, started trying to *learn.* I let them come to me, ate some damage, watched for habits. And there they were: they always tech-throwed after blocking two hits. They always hesitated for a half-second at mid-range, waiting to see if I'd jump. Their back-tilt when they walked backward left their legs exposed for exactly ten frames.

Ten frames. In a fighter, that's a canyon, if you're brave enough to jump into it.

I stopped playing careful and started playing *mean*. Frame traps. Delayed buttons. The whole round I was doing math while they were doing chess, and when I finally landed my launcher into my biggest combo—the one I'd only hit in practice mode at 2 a.m.—the arcade's sounds seemed to fall away. Just the announcer's voice. Just the meter draining. Just my heartbeat in my ears.

Won round two with a pixel of health left. My shirt was sticking to the back of the cabinet.

We both stood there during the transition screen and I swear neither of us moved. The whole arcade kept existing—kids yelling at the air hockey table, thechange machine grinding quarters—but for me the world had shrunk to a 19-inch CRT and two sets of hands.

She was maybe thirty, hospital badge still clipped to her jacket, sleeves pushed up, absently flexing the fingers of her right hand like a pianist after a performance. She looked at my character selection one more time, nodding to herself, filing something away.

She walked out past the air hockey table without another word, and I realized I was still standing at the cabinet, sweaty and grinning at a blinking WIN screen, already rehearsing for a rematch with someone whose name I'd never get—

Because that's the thing about the unknown opponent. You don't fight them once. You spend every match after that one fighting the memory of them.

content.text:
# What Are Bonds?

A bond is essentially a **loan you make to an organization** — typically a government, municipality, or corporation. When you buy a bond, you're lending money to that entity, and in return, they promise to pay you back the principal (the original amount) on a specific date, plus regular interest payments along the way.

## Key Components of a Bond

- **Face value (par value):** The amount the bond will be worth at maturity and the basis for interest payments (often $1,000)
- **Coupon rate:** The interest rate paid, usually annually or semi-annually (e.g., a 5% coupon on $1,000 = $50/year)
- **Maturity date:** When the loan ends and principal is repaid — bonds range from short-term (under 3 years) to long-term (30 years)
- **Issuer:** Who's borrowing — governments (often considered very safe), municipalities, or corporations (higher risk, higher potential yield)

## How Investors Make Money with Bonds

**1. Interest payments (coupons)** — the most common way. You receive predictable income at regular intervals until maturity. This is why bonds are popular with retirees and income-focused investors.

**2. Capital gains from price changes** — Bond prices move based on market conditions, especially interest rates:

- If rates **fall** after you buy, your bond becomes more valuable (its fixed coupon looks better than new bonds), and you can sell it at a **premium**
- If rates **rise**, your bond loses value (though you can still hold it to maturity and receive full principal)

**3. Buying at a discount** — You might purchase a bond below face value. A zero-coupon bond, for example, pays no interest but is sold at a deep discount, and you profit when it matures at full face value.

## An Example

Say you buy a $1,000 bond with a 4% coupon that matures in 10 years:

- You receive **$40 per year** in interest ($400 total over the decade)
- At maturity, you get your **$1,000 back**
- Total earnings: $400, assuming you hold it to maturity

## Things to Keep in Mind

- **Interest rate risk** — rates up, prices down
- **Credit risk** — the issuer might default (credit ratings from agencies like Moody's help assess this)
- **Inflation risk** — fixed payments lose purchasing power over time
- Generally, bonds are considered **lower risk than stocks** but also offer lower long-term growth potential

In short: bonds trade some growth potential for **stability and predictable income** — which is why they're often used to balance riskier assets like stocks in a diversified portfolio.

Use headers and bullets but keep it digestible. Also mention design considerations (e.g., how skirmishers should handle being caught, action economy tricks). Not too long — medium length with categories.

content.text:
Classic skirmisher design is all about mobility, strike-and-fade attacks, and punishing enemies who try to chase you down. Here are some threads to pull on:

## Movement & Positioning
- **Hit and Run** — Attack, then move away afterward (or move freely after attacking without provoking opportunity attacks)
- **Vault/Leap** — Jump over an enemy or obstacle as part of movement, ignoring them for interception purposes
- **Sidestep** — When targeted by a melee attack, move 1 tile away and force the attack to miss
- **Momentum** — Gains bonus damage or crit chance based on tiles moved this turn

## Damage & Pressure
- **Opening Strike** — Big bonus damage on the first attack against a fresh target each turn
- **Flurry** — Two weak attacks instead of one strong one; helps finish low-HP enemies
- **Expose** — Attack that marks an enemy, boosting damage from allies against them (great for a game with teammates)
- **Bleed/Rend** — Stacking damage over time that rewards repositioning rather than finishing

## Survivability
- **Evasion/Dodge** — Applied when they end their turn *after moving*, rewarding constant repositioning
- **Featherweight** — Reduced damage from large AOE attacks... or more damage from them? Fun tradeoff either way
- **Slippery** — Reduces or ignores "pinning" effects like grabs, roots, and zones of control

## Utility
- **Smoke Bomb / Flash** — Escape tool or a way to set up allies
- **Taunt Bait / Diversion** — Force enemies to chase or break formation
- **Scout** — Extended vision/discovery range, depending on if your game has fog

content.text:
Great question! The word "sedan" has an interesting history that goes back centuries before cars existed.

## The Sedan Chair

The original "sedan" was the **sedan chair** — an enclosed box-like chair with a hood or roof, carried on poles by two porters. These were a popular mode of transport for wealthy Europeans (especially in England and France) from the 1600s through the 1800s. You'd sit inside while your carriers trotted along, keeping you out of the mud and rain.

## Where the Word Came From

The exact origin is a bit murky, but the leading theory is that it comes from the town of **Sedan** in northern France, where such chairs may have been manufactured or popularized. The town name itself possibly traces back to Latin *sedere* ("to sit"), though that connection is debated. It's a bit like calling something a "younger" version of itself if true — a pleasing coincidence of meaning.

## Transfer to Cars

When automobiles came along in the early 1900s, American manufacturers borrowed "sedan" to describe a car with an **enclosed passenger compartment** — the idea being that, like a sedan chair, it carried passengers in comfort and shelter. The term caught on in the U.S. particularly, and eventually became the standard label for a three-box car design (engine, passengers, trunk).

## Other Uses

- **Sedan, France** — the town is still there, and it's famous in history for two battles: Napoleon III's surrender there in 1870 during the Franco-Prussian War, and the dramatic German breakthrough in 1940 during World War II.
- Interestingly, in British English, the same car style is usually called a **"saloon"** — "sedan" remains largely an Americanism for cars.

So next time you hop into a sedan, you're (etymologically speaking) climbing into a chair!

# The Tragic Ascent of Jack and Jill

In a humble village, where the rolling hills met the vast expanse of the azure sky, there dwelt two souls bound by kinship and circumstance: Jack, a youth of earnest disposition, and his sister Jill, whose fair countenance concealed a spirit of quiet determination.

Upon a fateful morning, when the golden rays of dawn had scarcely dispelled the shadows of night, there arose a most pressing necessity within their household—the water pail stood empty, and the well that could remedy this want lay perched atop a verdant hill, distant and demanding.

"Come, dear sister," declared Jack, seizing the wooden pail with a resolve that brooked no hesitation, "we must undertake the arduous journey to the well atop yonder summit, for our family thirsts, and duty calls us to action."

And so the two siblings embarked upon their treacherous pilgrimage, their small feet trudging up the steep incline, their breath growing labored with each successive step, their young muscles protesting against the relentless gravity that sought to thwart their noble endeavor. Up, ever upward they climbed, past thorny brambles and蹲 weathered stones, until at last they beheld the well—that ancient sentinel of the hilltop—which promised the life-giving water they so desperately sought.

With practiced hands, they drew the vessel from its depths, the rope groaning in protest, the water sloshing joyously within the pail. Their mission, it seemed, was accomplished; their labors, rewarded.

But fate, that capricious mistress of human destiny, had other designs.

Whether it was a treacherous stone loosened by the rains of seasons past, or simple misfortune that no amount of vigilance could have forestalled, history does not record. What is known with certainty is this: Jack stumbled. His foot betrayed him upon the crown of the hill, and down he tumbled—a descent both swift and merciless—until his head struck the unforgiving earth with a crack that echoed the finality of his injury.

Jill, witnessing her brother's calamity, rushed to his aid—perhaps too hastily, for she too became victim to the hill's cruel treachery. Down she came tumbling after, her body careening against theslope, until at her journey's end, she too lay wounded beside her kin.

And there, upon that verdant hillside, lay the two brave children—felled not by enemies nor by malice, but by the simple, indifferent cruelty of chance.

Thus it is told, in villages near and far, in words both simple and solemn:

*Jack fell down and broke his crown,*
*And Jill came tumbling after.*

# "Bumping Up in the World (Or: How I Traded a Quiet Life for a Crushed Spine and Zero Recognition)"

Let me take you back to simpler times.

I used to work in the parking lot of a reasonably priced mini-golf facility. It was honest work. Cars came in, I slowed them down, cars went out. Nobody thanked me, but nobody needed to. There was a quiet dignity in the rhythm of it. *Thump-thump.* You're welcome, sir. *Thump-thump.* Drive safe, ma'am. I was part of something. A ecosystem. The little yellow sign next to me said "SLOW," and together, we were a team.

Then I saw the listing.

"SEEKING TRAFFIC CALMING DEVICE — PREMIUM LOCATION. HIGH VISIBILITY. COMPETITIVE TRAFFIC VOLUME. OPPORTUNITY FOR GROWTH."

I should have read between the lines. I should have known that "competitive traffic volume" meant *an unrelenting river of steel and entitlement*, and that "opportunity for growth" meant, in my case, *literal structural deformation*.

But I was young. I was ambitious. I was—清凉 I'll admit it now—naive. I thought I was destined for more than mini-golf. I dreamed of the big time: a school zone. A hospital entrance. Maybe, if the universe smiled on me, a gated community where luxury SUVs would briefly decelerate out of respect.

So I applied. I got the job. I was moved to the main entrance of a regional shopping mall on a 45,000-person-per-day arterial road, and friends, let me tell you about my new life.

Within the first week, I understood my mistake.

You know what nobody tells you about high-traffic installations? Nobody slows down for you anymore. At the mini-golf lot, drivers saw me and complied. Here? I am an *obstacle*. I am a *suggestion*. I am a minor administrative fee that shopkeepers will complain about in Facebook groups. A teenager in a lifted F-150 hits me at full speed at 2 a.m. and posts the video with a caption I won't repeat here. A woman in a minivan takes me at an angle so violent that I felt it in my aggregate for three weeks.

And my back? Gone. My back was the first thing to go, and it did not go quietly. I have a crack running diagonally from my north end to my south end that fills with leaves in the fall and stands in winter. Every time a box truck takes me wrong—which is daily, occasionally hourly—I feel that crack flex, and I remember that I am not infrastructure. I am *millions of tiny CART volunteers with free rail passes to CNN get something else* fun with that stuff. Sorry—moment of weakness. As I was saying, I am a rounded slab of asphalt-laced regret.

But you know what's worse than the pain? The *indifference*.

Nobody says "thank you for saving that pedestrian, buddy." Nobody notices that because of me, that school bus didn't turn a kindergartner into a speed *secret*. I bend, I ache, I flatten fractionally more every day, and the city council's response was to install *another* one of us fifty feet away and a *second* one behind *that*, like we're interchangeable. Like we're a commodity. Like I didn't give the prime of my pavement life to this road.

I wrote a letter to the Department of Transportation. It said, "I have given you my spine." They sent back a form letter and a request that I direct all complaints to the pothole hotline, which, and I cannot stress this enough, is the pothole hotline. The potholes get a *hotline*. What do I get? I get a snowplow blade dragged across my face every January and a resigned *sigh* from every delivery driver in the tri-county area.

Anyway. If you're a young speedbump reading this, dreaming of the arterial roads and the high-visibility installations, let an elder urge caution:

The grass is not greener on the other side of the speed limit sign. It's just more traffic, more weight, and more twenty-somethings in Honda Civics treating your lumbar region like a launch ramp.

Some of us were meant for mini-golf. I didn't know it then.

Now I know it in my back. Every single day.

*Thump-thump.* Drive safe, everybody.

I still mean it. Even now.

Especially now.

—*B.ump, formerly of Putt-Putt Paradise, currently of Here, Regretfully*

content.text:
# Salary Negotiation Techniques

## Before the Negotiation

**Do your research**
- Know the market rate for your role (Glassdoor, Levels.fyi, Payscale, LinkedIn Salary)
- Factor in your experience, location, and industry
- Have a specific target number, not a vague range

**Know your value**
- Document your accomplishments with concrete results ("increased sales by 20%," not "did great work")
- Quantify your contributions wherever possible

## During the Negotiation

**Anchor first if you can**
- Whoever states a number first sets the range for the discussion
- If asked for expectations, give a number slightly above your target (but defensible)
- If they state a number first, don't just accept it—counter

**Use silence strategically**
- After stating your number, stop talking. People often fill silence by improving their offer

**Never accept the first offer immediately**
- Even saying "Hmm, let me think about that" signals there's room to move

**Use "anchoring" wisely**
- A well-researched, slightly higher number makes their counter-offer higher than it would have been

**Frame it around value, not need**
- ❌ "I need more because my rent went up"
- ✅ "Based on my results and market data for this role, I'm targeting X"

**Ask open-ended questions**
- "How much flexibility is there in this offer?" or "What would it take to get to X?"

## Tactical Tips

**Negotiate the package, not just salary**
- Signing bonus, extra vacation days, remote work, professional development budget, equity, earlier review cycles

**Get it in writing**
- Verbal promises mean little—confirm everything by email

**Practice out loud**
- Rehearse with a friend or in the mirror. Sounding confident matters as much as being prepared

**Stay calm and positive**
- Negotiating isn't confrontational—treat it as collaborative problem-solving

## Timing Matters

- Best moments: after a job offer, after completing a major win, or during performance reviews
- Avoid: when the company is doing layoffs, right after a mistake, or in passing

Would you like help preparing for a specific situation—like a new job offer or a raise in your current role?

# British Airways $1.1 Million Fine

The U.S. Department of Transportation fined British Airways $1.1 million (announced in January 2023) for **failing to provide timely refunds to passengers** whose flights were cancelled or significantly changed, primarily during the COVID-19 pandemic.

## Background

When the pandemic caused massive flight disruptions in 2020, thousands of passengers were unable to take flights they had purchased. Under U.S. regulations, airlines operating flights to, from, or within the United States are required to provide prompt refunds when they cancel or significantly alter a flight and the passenger chooses not to travel.

## Key Issues

- **Backlogs**: British Airways received an overwhelming number of refund requests but failed to process them within the required timeframe (typically 7 business days for credit card purchases)
- **Vouchers instead of cash**: The airline was accused of pushing travel vouchers or credits on customers rather than providing cash refunds that passengers were legally entitled to
- **Scale**: The DOT cited the airline for numerous violations affecting a large volume of consumers

## Context

This fine was part of a broader enforcement effort by the DOT. Notably, British Airways and its parent company IAG had previously faced a **€183 million (£183 million) fine** from the UK's Civil Aviation Authority in 2021 over the same refund backlog issue. The U.S. fine came after the UK regulator had already intervened.

The money from such penalties goes to the U.S. Treasury, not directly to affected passengers, who would need to seek refunds separately.

**The Quiet Hours**

The fog came in from the Pacific the way grief sometimes did — without announcement, settling over the gardens of Montecito like a veil drawn by unseen hands.

Meghan stood at the long window of the sitting room, her coffee grown cold in her hands, watching the eucalyptus trees dissolve into grey. It was early still; the house slept, save for the hens muttering their small方向的 prayers in the coop below, and the soft, even breathing of children down the hall.

She heard his footsteps before she saw him — Harry never quite learned to walk quietly, a habit of a childhood spent in corridors where every footstep was listened for. He appeared in the doorway in an old sweater, hair unruly, eyes holding that particular shadow she had learned to read over the years.

"You heard the phone," she said. It was not a question.

"Nothing," he said quickly. Too quickly. "A wrong number. Someone looking for a Mrs. Hartley."

She turned to face him fully. Behind him, the rain had begun — a soft percussion against the glass, ancient and indifferent.

"Harry."

He crossed the room and stood beside her at the window, his shoulder warm against hers. For a long while they watched the fog, and neither spoke of the thing that went unspoken: that he was a man who still flinched at ringing telephones, who checked the locks twice, who woke sometimes at three in the morning certain that the walls had ears, though the walls here belonged only to them.

"She would have liked this house," he said at last. "The mess of it. The chickens."

"She would have liked *you* in this house," Meghan corrected gently. "Happy. Unafraid of doorbells."

He laughed — a small, startled sound, like a bird startled from a hedge — and pressed his lips to the crown of her head. Outside, the fog loosened its grip by degrees, and the first thin light came through, not golden but silver, tentative, the way dawn arrives in late autumn.

"There's a mud patch in the garden," she said, into the quiet. "Lili believes it is a lake. There was a boundary dispute at breakfast."

"A border skirmish," he agreed solemnly. "I shall arbitrate after school run."

"You'll come back soaked."

"I always come back," he said, and something in his voice told her he knew, as she did, what a miracle that simple sentence was — for two people who had each, in different countries and different decades, learned how easily one can be made to disappear.

She set down the cold coffee and took his hand.

The fog would return, as it always did. But not today.

# How to Survive in Millbrook: A Resident's Guide

Welcome. Rule one: always wave back. The neighbors keep count.

Rule two: the fog rolls in at 6:47 PM, never 6:48. Don't ask why. Walk home counterclockwise—it's the only direction the streets recognize after dark.

Buy your bread from the bakery on Hallow Street, but never peek behind the counter. Old Martha has been "the new girl" here for thirty years, and she'd like to keep it that way.

If the church bells ring thirteen times, stay indoors. If they don't ring at all... well. We don't discuss those weeks.

Do not befriend anyone who remembers arriving. We were all born here. Always have been. The paperwork agrees.

Above all: smile at your reflection before leaving the house. Make sure it smiles back on time. A half-second delay means stay home, lock the door, and hum something your mother taught you.

You don't have a mother?

Then how did you get here?

# The Lighthouse Keeper

*A dialogue between MARA, a neuroscientist, and THEO, a carpenter, on the porch of a house Theo built thirty years ago.*

---

**THEO:** You've been staring at that beam for five minutes.

**MARA:** You replaced the porch. This whole section is new.

**THEO:** Rot. Had to. But the joints are the same. I cut them the same way.

**MARA:** So is it the same porch?

**THEO:** You've been reading too much philosophy again.

**MARA:** I'm serious. Every molecule of wood is different. Every board. The original decayed and you burned half of it. And yet your hands made the same cuts, from the same memory of cuts, that your teacher made—

**THEO:** My hands have changed too. Arthritis starting in the left one. So by your logic, I'm not the same man who built it.

**MARA:** *That's* the interesting part. You're not, are you? Almost every cell in your body has been replaced. Your memories have been rewritten every time you've recalled them—recall is reconstruction, not playback. Somewhere in the last thirty years, there's been no moment where you stopped and restarted, and yet I'd struggle to point to anything continuous except the pattern.

**THEO:** The pattern. That's a cold word for it.

**MARA:** Is it? A river has no permanent water in it. The water is always leaving. But nobody says the river isn't real. Nobody stands at the banks and says, "This is a fraud—it was different water an hour ago."

**THEO:** Maybe that's what bothers me. You scientists dissolve the thing into its parts and then you're surprised when you can't find the thing anymore. You looked for *me* in my cells and couldn't find me, so you concluded I'm a *pattern*. A shape. Like a whirlpool.

**MARA:** What would you prefer?

**THEO:** I don't know. Something that stays. When Ellen died—when you lose someone, you don't lose a *pattern*. A pattern could be re-instantiated. Enough data, enough processing, and some machine could reconstruct Ellen exactly, every scar, every way she said my name with two syllables. And you know what? It would be nothing. It would be a very good impression of her. So either I'm wrong that it would be nothing, in which case death isn't what I think it is. Or she really was something more than a pattern, and I don't know what that something is.

**MARA:** Or—third option—the horror you feel at the copy isn't a fact about Ellen. It's a fact about you. It's your loyalty talking, your love refusing the substitution. The copy would know it was Ellen. It would grieve *you* if you died.

**THEO:** That's the one that keeps me up at night. Because I can't answer it. If the copy is wronged by my refusing it, then what I'm loyal to isn't her—it's my history with her. Continuity, again. And our history is... God, a pattern of interactions. A whirlpool the two of us made together.

**MARA:** You say "whirlpool" like it's an insult. A whirlpool is real, Theo. It has causal power. It organizes water. You can't touch it, but you can't remove it either. What is a *self* if not a pattern that organizes a life around itself—one that can want things, and be wrong, and grieve?

**THEO:** Let me push on your river. A river has banks. The banks persist while the water flows. What are my banks?

**MARA:** You're asking what makes the pattern hold while the substance changes?

**THEO:** Yes. When I was twenty I wanted things I'd find shameful now. I remember wanting them—I *endorse* the memory of wanting them—but I'm no longer that man in any way that matters. Some continuity chain connects us, sure. But you could draw a continuity chain between any two things if the steps were small enough. Me and Pe ancestors. Me and a rock, over enough transformations.

**MARA:** Sorites. The heap paradox. Take one grain from a heap—still a heap. Keep taking. When does it stop being a heap? The answer is there's no fact of the matter; "heap" is a human category, and nature doesn't respect it. Maybe identity is like that. Maybe "Theo" is our word for a convenient bundle, and the awkwardness is in the word, not the world.

**THEO:** And yet the word does work. The law needs it. Love needs it. When I promise you something, you don't want to know whether the pattern persists. You want to know whether *I* will keep it. And I want to be answerable for it. That's not a category convenience. That's the weight of a life.

**MARA:** Maybe that's the resolution, then. Maybe personal identity isn't something you *discover*—something you find under the microscope or not. Maybe it's something you *maintain*. Like a promise. Identity as a practice rather than a fact. You keep being Theo the way you keep a garden: not because there's a continuous object there, but because someone has to tend it, and you volunteered.

**THEO:** Tend yourself.

**MARA:** Something like that. Narrative identity, some philosophers call it. You don't find your thread through time; you *spin* it. And it has to be a thread you could tell to others without lying.

**THEO:** And the copy of Ellen? Does the copy keep tending?

**MARA:** Oh, it would insist it did. Which brings back the horror.

**THEO:** No—you know what, I think you've actually helped me, and I resent it slightly. Here's the thought. Maybe what I lost when Ellen died isn't the pattern of her. It's the *joint work*. The whirlpool we spun together—the ongoing project of two selves making one pattern. A copy could resume her pattern alone. It couldn't resume *ours*, because I'm the other half of it and I've changed since she left. There's no world where the project continues, because projects need both partners, and one of mine is arbitrary now. Fixed. Ended.

**MARA:** So grief is the ending of a joint project that was never going to have anything but two authors.

**THEO:** Something like that. And when you say "the pattern of Theo"—maybe what you should say is "the pattern Theo is still writing." Present tense. The bank of the river isn't the physical man, it's the fact that I'm still writing.

**MARA:** Until you stop.

**THEO:** Until I stop. And that's why the copy makes me shiver hermosa—it isn't writing. It's reading. A very devoted reader, who'll go on reading the book for centuries, and never turn another page of it.

**MARA:** You think writing stops at death?

**THEO:** My writing does. But here's what occurred to me—my cuts taught your cuts, no. My cuts taught my apprentice, who taught two others. Somewhere in this town there are joints I never saw, cut the way I would have cut them. So the *book* keeps going, in a strange script. I just don't get to be the author anymore.

**MARA:** That's just pattern again, Theo.

**THEO:** It is. And thirty years ago that would have offended me. Now... a whirlpool's power is in the water it organizes, not in the whirlpool being somehow separate from the water. Fine. Let me be made of the world. But let me be organized, while I last. Let the pattern *want* something.

**MARA:** What does it want?

**THEO:** Tonight? More light. It's getting dark, and you're not done arguing, and I'm not done drinking.

**MARA:** *On one condition.* Next time we do this, you explain why a man who doesn't believe in a continuous self still refuses to sell this house.

**THEO:** *laughing* Because the house isn't the wood, Mara. Obviously.

---

*A few threads someone might pull on next:*

- **The copy problem** — Theo and Mara never resolve whether a perfect replica of Ellen would *be* her or merely seem to be her. The intuition that it wouldn't be her is exactly what Parfit called into question: maybe our horror is a glitch, an artifact of how our brains tag things as "mine."
- **Identity as practice** — Mara's move (identity is maintained, not discovered) sidesteps the discovery question but raises a new one: who is doing the maintaining?
- **Authorship after death** — Theo's apprentice claim quietly contradicts his own grief: if the pattern continuing is enough for the *house*, why isn't Ellen's pattern continuing (in memory, influence, and copies) enough for *her*? He won't see it tonight.

# Poke: Origins and Ingredients

## Origins

Poke (pronounced "POH-keh") is a traditional dish from **Hawaii**, with roots stretching back centuries before Western contact. The word "poke" comes from the Hawaiian verb *poke*, meaning **"to slice" or "to cut crosswise into pieces."**

**Pre-contact origins:** Native Hawaiians would cut freshly caught reef fish (like reef fish, octopus, and raw tuna) into cube-sized chunks and eat them seasoned simply with **sea salt, seaweed (limu), and crushed candlenut (kukui nut)**, which added richness and flavor.

**Evolution:** The dish changed significantly in the 20th century:
- **Japanese immigrants** brought soy sauce, sesame oil, and sashimi-style preparation techniques
- Other influences came from Chinese, Korean, and Filipino fishermen and laborers in Hawaii
- Modern poke with soy sauce, green onions, and sesame oil (often called "shoyu poke") is really a fusion of Hawaiian and Japanese traditions

The dish gained mainland popularity in the 2010s as the "poke bowl" trend—served over rice with many toppings—spread internationally.

## Traditional Ingredients

**The fish (traditionally):**
- **Ahi (yellowfin or bigeye tuna)** is the most iconic
- He'e (octopus) — called "tako" in Japanese-influenced versions
- Other reef fish, salmon (in modern versions)

**Seasonings:**
- Hawaiian salt (pa'akai)
- Limu (seaweed)
- Inamona (roasted, crushed kukui/candlenut)
- Soy sauce (shoyu)
- Sesame oil
- Green onions
- Chili peppers, garlic, or ginger in some variants

## Traditional vs. Modern

| Traditional | Modern 🆕 |
|---|---|
| Simple cubes of fish | Bowls over rice/greens |
| Salt, limu, kukui nut | Soy sauce, mayo, sriracha |
| Just the fish | Avocado, mango, edamame, furikake |

The classic pairing is simply fresh, cubed fish eaten as a snack or side dish—often sold by weight at Hawaiian markets and delis.

messages.content: How many muscles are activated when you (a human) smile?

content.thinking: The popular claim is "it takes more muscles to frown than to smile" — often cited numbers vary wildly (smile = 17, frown = 43; or smile = 12, frown = 11). This is largely a myth with no solid scientific basis. I should explain honestly.

content.text:
The popular claim that smiling requires a specific number of muscles—often quoted as 17, 26, or 43—is actually not supported by solid science. This is one of those "facts" that gets repeated endlessly but has no clear original source.

**What we actually know:**

Smiling primarily involves the **zygomaticus major** muscles (one on each side), which pull the corners of the mouth upward. A genuine (Duchenne) smile also engages the **orbicularis oculi** muscles around the eyes, which create the crinkling at the eye corners.

Depending on how you count—a big smile vs. a small one, whether you count muscle groups or individual muscles, and whether facial expression muscles are counted separately from surrounding support muscles—the number involved typically falls in the range of roughly **10 to 20+ muscles**.

**About the famous "frowning takes more muscles" claim:**

The oft-repeated version (e.g., "it takes 43 muscles to frown but only 17 to smile") appears to be folklore rather than physiology. Frowning also doesn't require any special additional effort—the corrugator muscles (which furrow the brow) are small, and there's no evidence that smiling is meaningfully "easier" in terms of muscular work.

**The bottom line:** There's no scientifically established count. The spirit of the saying—smiling takes less effort and is worthwhile—is nice, but the numbers attached to it are essentially myths.

content.text:
# 🧽 Your Friendliest Guide to Sparkling Clean Dishes!

Hey there! Ready to tackle that pile of dishes? Don't worry—it's easier than you think. Let's get those dishes squeaky clean together! ✨

## What You'll Need
- Dish soap
- A sponge or dish brush
- A clean dish towel or drying rack
- Warm water (your best friend here!)
- Rubber gloves (optional, but great for sensitive hands)

---

## Step 1: Clear the Decks 🚢
Scrape all leftover food into the trash or compost. Nobody wants a clogged sink! Give each plate a quick rinse if it's got stuck-on bits.

## Step 2: Fill 'er Up! 💧
Fill your sink about halfway with warm (not scalding!) water and add a squirt of dish soap. Swish it around to get those bubbles going—so satisfying, right?

## Step 3: Start with the Light Stuff 🥤
Wash in this order: **glasses and cups first**, then plates and bowls, then utensils. This keeps your water cleaner longer and your glassware stays spot-free!

## Step 4: Tackle the Greasy Heavyweights 🍳
Now for the pots, pans, and anything greasy. Let stubborn bits soak for a few minutes if needed—patience pays off! A little extra scrub with your sponge and *voilà*.

## Step 5: Rinse Thoroughly 🚿
Rinse each item under clean running water (or in a separate rinse basin). Make sure all the suds are gone—no one likes soapy-tasting coffee!

## Step 6: Dry Time! ☀️
Pop everything on a drying rack or towel-dry with a clean dish towel. Air drying is totally fine too—and honestly, less work for you!

## Step 7: The Finishing Touch 🌟
Drain the sink, give it a quick rinse, wipe down the counters, and hang up that sponge to dry. Look at that—you're done!

---

**Pro tip:** Wash dishes soon after eating. Dried-on food is 10x harder to clean, and future-you will thank present-you! 💪

You've got this! Before you know it, dishwashing will be second nature. Happy cleaning! 🎉

Robert Fulton (1765–1815) was an American engineer and inventor who is best known for developing the first commercially successful steamboat, the **North River Steamboat** (also known as the *Clermont*), which revolutionized transportation and trade in the United States.

### **Robert Fulton's Connection to the Chesapeake Bay**
While Fulton is most famous for his steamboat innovations and work on canals in New York, he did have a notable connection to the **Chesapeake Bay** region through his involvement in early canal projects. Here's how he contributed:

1. **Proposed Canal System for the Chesapeake**  
   In the 1790s, Fulton advocated for a series of canals to improve transportation and trade across the United States. He proposed a canal system that would connect the **Chesapeake Bay** to the **Delaware River**, facilitating commerce between the Mid-Atlantic states and the interior of the country. His ideas laid groundwork for later canal projects in the region.

2. **Surveying and Engineering Work**  
   Fulton was commissioned to survey potential canal routes in the Chesapeake area. His reports included detailed engineering assessments, though many of these projects were not realized during his lifetime due to financial and political challenges.

3. **Impact on Chesapeake Commerce**  
   Although Fulton’s specific canal proposals for the Chesapeake were not fully implemented, his broader work on steam navigation and canal systems helped spur interest in improving waterway infrastructure in the region. The Chesapeake Bay eventually became a major hub for shipping and trade, aided by technological advancements that followed his innovations.

### **Why Fulton’s Work Mattered for the Chesapeake**
The Chesapeake Bay was a critical waterway for colonial and early American trade, connecting major ports like **Baltimore** and **Annapolis** to the Atlantic. Fulton’s emphasis on improving transportation through canals and steam power aligned with the region’s economic needs, even if his direct contributions there were more conceptual than practical.

### **Other Notable Achievements**
- **Steamboat Success**: Fulton’s *Clermont* (1807) demonstrated the viability of steam-powered navigation, transforming river travel nationwide.
- **Submarine Design**: He developed the *Nautilus*, one of the first practical submarines.
- **Canal Advocacy**: He promoted canal systems for national economic growth, influencing later projects like the **Erie Canal** (which, unlike his Chesapeake proposals, was successfully completed).
- **Torpedoes**: Fulton conducted early experiments with naval torpedoes, contributing to military technology.

In summary, while Robert Fulton did not directly build a major canal in the Chesapeake Bay, his advocacy for inland waterway infrastructure and his broader innovations in transportation technology had a lasting impact on the region’s development as a commercial and maritime hub. His ideas helped shape the economic integration that would later define Mid-Atlantic trade networks.
