**The Cocoa Tin**

Eleven-year-old Marcus had inherited his grandfather's ancient cocoa tin the month before—a dented, rust-freckled thing that had once held loose change and now held the beginnings of his own coin collection. Grandpa had taught him the basics before the hospital visits took over: how to hold a coin by its edges, how to read a date through a magnifying glass, how some pennies were worth far more than a cent. "It's all about rarity, kid," Grandpa had said. "The rare ones have stories."

Marcus spent whole Saturdays hunched over his desk, sorting through rolls of pennies borrowed from the bank. Most were ordinary—2010s, 1990s, dull copper discs he filed into cardboard albums by decade. But Grandpa had drilled the magic words into him: 1909-S VDB. 1914-D. 1922 plain. The key dates, the grails that every collector chased. Marcus had memorized the list like spelling words, though he privately figured he'd never see one, not in a million wheat cents.

Then, one rainy Tuesday in March, he opened the last roll of the afternoon. As he slid the coins across his blue felt mat, one penny stopped him cold. It was dark, nearly chocolate-colored, and heavy with age. His hands trembled as he raised the magnifier. "1914," he whispered, his heart slamming against his ribs. Then he saw it—a small "D" beneath the date. Denver. He checked the list taped to his desk. His eyes went wide. A 1914-D. One of the rarest Lincoln pennies in existence.

Marcus ran to the phone and called Grandpa, breathless, reading off the date and mintmark twice to make sure. There was a long pause on the line, and then a quiet, happy laugh. "Well, kid," Grandpa said, "you're officially a collector now." Marcus placed the penny gently into its own cardboard flip, and for the first time, he understood: the tin had been passed to exactly the right person.

One of his eyes resembled that of a vulture — a pale blue eye, with a film over it. Whenever it fell upon me, my blood ran cold; and so by degrees — very gradually — I made up my mind to take the life of the old man, and thus rid myself of the eye forever.

Now this is the point. You fancy me mad. Madmen know nothing. But you should have seen me. You should have seen how wisely I proceeded — with what caution — with what foresight — with what dissimulation I went to work! I was never kinder to the old man than during the whole week before I killed him. And every night, about midnight, I turned the latch of his door and opened it — oh, so gently! And then, when I had made an opening sufficient for my head, I put in a dark lantern, all closed, closed, so that no light shone out, and then I thrust in my head. Oh, you would have laughed to see how cunningly I thrust it in! I moved it slowly — very, very slowly, so that I might not disturb the old man’s sleep. It took me an hour to place my whole head within the opening so far that I could see him as he lay upon his bed. Ha! — would a madman have been so wise as this? And then, when my head was well in the room, I undid the lantern cautiously — oh, so cautiously — cautiously (for the hinges creaked) — I undid it just so much that a single thin ray fell upon the vulture eye. And this I did for seven long nights — every night just at midnight — but I found the eye always closed; and so it was impossible to do the work; for it was not the old man who vexed me, but his Evil Eye. And every morning, when the day broke, I went boldly into the chamber, and spoke courageously to him, calling him by name in a hearty tone, and inquiring how he had passed the night. So you see he would have been a very profound old man, indeed, to suspect that every night, just at twelve, I looked in upon him while he slept.

He insists he is not mad. He repeats it, in fact, with a kind of feverish pride — he is nervous, yes, dreadfully nervous, tremulous even as he speaks — but this, he argues, is proof of his sanity rather than against it. The disease, he claims, has not dulled his senses but sharpened them, particularly his hearing. He says he heard all things in the heavens and the earth; he says he heard things in hell. And having said this much, he gestures, wide-eyed and unsettlingly composed, for one to listen and judge for oneself how healthily he can tell the whole story.

He cannot say how the idea first came to him, and one watches him reach for it like a man grasping in the dark. He admits it had no reason behind it: no passion, no grudge, no greed. He loved the old man, he insists — he had never been wronged, never insulted. It was the eye. One of the old man's eyes, he says, resembled that of a vulture — a pale blue eye, filmed over like something dead — and whenever it fell upon him, his blood ran cold. Watching him recount it, one notices his voice quicken around the word *eye*. By degrees, he explains — very gradually — he made up his mind to kill the old man and rid himself of it forever.

He knows what his listener is thinking. He pauses here, leaning forward, as though this is the point upon which everything turns: a madman is reckless, a madman knows nothing. But one should have seen him, he says — should have seen how wisely he proceeded, with what caution, what foresight, what dissimulation. He is eager, almost childlike in his need to be admired for it.

He was never kinder to the old man, he claims, than during the whole week before the murder. Each night at midnight, he crept to the old man's door and turned the latch — so gently, he emphasizes, demonstrating with a careful twist of his hand. He opened it just wide enough for his head, then slid a dark lantern through, shuttered so that not a ray escaped, and then he thrust his own head inside. At this he almost laughs, asking whether one would not have laughed too to see how cunningly he did it — how very, very slowly he moved, so as not to disturb the old man's sleep. It took him an hour, he says, to place his whole head within the opening, far enough to see the old man upon his bed. A madman? Would a madman have been so wise? His face demands the answer.

Then, when his head was well within the room, he undid the lantern — cautiously, so cautiously, ever so cautiously, for the hinges creaked — just enough that a single thin ray fell upon the vulture eye. Seven long nights he did this, every night at midnight. But the eye was always closed. And so the deed was impossible, he explains, as if the logic were immaculate: it was not the old man who vexed him, but his Evil Eye. Never once, in all those nights, did the old man suspect anything — for every morning, the narrator went boldly into his chamber and spoke courageously to him, calling him by name in a hearty tone, inquiring how he had slept.

He recounts all of this with evident satisfaction. Every night, just at twelve, he says — pausing, savoring it — he looked in upon the old man while he slept. And he waits, one suspects, for the listener to share in his wonder at how clever he has been.

content.text:
# Screen-Free Summer Week: Indoor Activity Plan

Here's a full week of activities that work across the 5–10 age range. I've built in a daily structure so you're not scrambling for ideas.

## Monday: Art Studio Day
- **Morning:** "Mystery art challenge" — pull random prompts from a hat (draw an animal wearing a hat, build a sculpture from foil, paint with cotton balls)
- **Afternoon:** Collaborative mural on a big sheet of paper taped to the wall
- **Age tip:** The 5-year-old gets the foil/free draw; the older two can attempt timed challenges with the older kids' prompts

## Tuesday: Building & Engineering Day
- Blanket fort construction (big hit with all ages — let them plan the "blueprint" first)
- Cup stacking challenges or Domino runs
- Marshmallow-and-toothpick towers — competition: tallest freestanding structure

## Wednesday: Kitchen Science Day
- Baking soda + vinegar volcanoes
- Make oobleck (cornstarch + water) — always a crowd-pleaser
- Invisible ink with lemon juice and a lamp
- **Age tip:** Older kids can "run" experiments for the 5-year-old, which keeps them engaged too

## Thursday: Performance Day
- Morning: Write a short play or puppet show together (dig out old socks for puppets)
- Afternoon: Rehearse, design tickets and a "stage," perform for parents at pickup
- Freeze dance and karaoke (no screens needed — just music)

## Friday:挣钱--I mean, Indoor Carnival
- They spend the morning building carnival games (beanbag toss, ring toss with paper plates, bowling with water bottles)
- Afternoon: Run the "carnival" with tickets and small prizes (stickers, choosing the afternoon snack)
- This one eats up huge chunks of time with setup

## Backup fillers for any day
- Indoor scavenger hunt (write rhyme-based clues for older kids, picture clues for the 5-year-old)
- Card/board games:Uno, Memory, andQueryBuilder-style games work across ages
- Story chain: each kid adds a sentence to a story, then write it down and illustrate
- Sensory bins or "mystery box" guessing games for the 5-year-old

## General tips
- **Build in quiet time** — after lunch, everyone does independent reading or quiet puzzles for 30–45 minutes (the 5-year-old can look at picture books)
- **Rotate "group" and "own" activities** — the 10-year-old especially will want independent time
- **Keep an "I'm bored" jar** — fill it with 20 quick activities written on slips of paper and have them draw when they hit a lull

Want me to expand any of these days into hour-by-hour schedules, or suggest low-cost supply lists for the craft-heavy days?

content.text:
Pizza rolls were created by **Jeno Paulucci** in 1968. Paulucci, an Italian-American entrepreneur, had previously founded Chun King, a canned Chinese food company, and later Jeno's Frozen Foods.

The story goes that he adapted the concept of the egg roll—using fried dough wrapped around a filling—but swapped in pizza ingredients like tomato sauce, cheese, and pepperoni. He called them "pizza rolls" and produced them through his Jeno's brand.

In 1985, Paulucci sold Jeno's to Pillsbury, which rebranded the product as **Totino's Pizza Rolls**, connecting it to the Totino's brand (founded by Rose and James Totino) that Pillsbury had acquired in 1977. Totino's Pizza Rolls remain a popular frozen snack to this day.

content.text:
President James A. Garfield was shot on **July 2, 1881**, at the Baltimore and Potomac Railroad Station in Washington, D.C. He was only four months into his presidency at the time.

The shooter was Charles J. Guiteau, a disgruntled office-seeker who believed he was owed a diplomatic post. Garfield did not die immediately—he lingered for over two months while doctors (famously using unsanitary methods that likely worsened his condition) tried to treat him. He died on September 19, 1881, in Elberon, New Jersey. Guiteau was convicted of murder and executed in June 1882.

**Lily and the Sunblossom**

Lily was ten years old, with a cascade of golden hair that tumbled past her waist and wide green eyes that sparkled with endless curiosity. Much like her favorite storybook heroines, she spent her days painting murals on the garden fence, chasing butterflies, and dreaming of adventures beyond her small village. She was kind to everyone she met—even the grumpy old baker who never smiled—and she believed deeply that no problem was too big when you faced it with courage and a loyal heart.

One misty morning, while exploring the far corner of her backyard, Lily discovered a flower she had never seen before. It glowed with a warm, golden light, its petals shimmering like captured sunlight. When she gently touched it, warmth flowed through her fingers, and she felt stronger, braver, and lighter than ever before. The old garden book in her grandmother's attic revealed its name: the Sunblossom, a legendary flower that granted the power of healing light and boundless courage to anyone with a pure heart.

Lily barely had time to marvel at her discovery before trouble struck. An army of goblins, wicked and green-skinned, came marching down from the mountains, threatening to destroy the village and steal everything the villagers held dear. The townspeople hid behind locked doors, terrified, but Lily refused to let fear win. Clutching the Sunblossom, she raced toward the village square, her long hair streaming behind her like a golden banner.

Standing tall before the goblin horde, Lily raised the flower high and sang the gentle lullaby her mother had taught her—the only thing she knew that felt as brave as she felt. The Sunblossom blazed to life, sending waves of radiant light across the village. The goblins, creatures of shadow and spite, couldn't bear the glow. They shrieked and scattered, fleeing back into the mountains from which they came.

The villagers emerged, cheering, and lifted Lily onto their shoulders. She smiled, tucking the Sunblossom safely into her hair, knowing that true magic had never been in the flower at all—it had been inside her all along.

content.text:
**What is a nudity clause?**

Sometimes, when actors make movies or TV shows, a character needs to appear without clothes on. Before any filming happens, the actor gets a special paper to sign called a "nudity clause." This paper explains exactly when the actor will need to take off clothes, how much will be shown, and how it will be filmed.

The most important thing about this paper is that the actor gets to decide. Nobody can force an actor to take off their clothes if they don't want to. The actor can say "no," or they can say, "I'm okay with this part, but not that part." If the actor signs the paper, it means they agree to it — but they can also change their mind later if they feel uncomfortable.

There are also special helpers on movie sets whose whole job is to make sure actors feel safe and respected during these scenes. If someone breaks the rules in the contract, the actor can take them to court.

In short: a nudity clause is a promise on paper that keeps actors in charge of their own bodies.

content.text:
# The Pigeons of Fifth Avenue

## A Rough Draft

Geraldinius P. Featherworth III — known to his friends as Gerald, and to everyone else as *that pigeon who thinks he's better than us* — considered himself the finest bird in all of Manhattan.

He lived on the ledge of a very important building on Fifth Avenue, the kind with a doorman and gold letters on the window. Gerald did not eat off the sidewalk. Gerald did not peck at discarded pizza crusts like some *common street pigeon*. Gerald breakfasted daily at the diamond-shaped plaza a few blocks down, where an elderly woman named Mrs. Wexler fed the birds bagel pieces from a white paper bag, and Gerald always — *always* — got the everything bagel. Because everything bagels were for pigeons of *distinction*.

"Plain bagels," he liked to announce, swinging his iridescent green-purple head importantly, "are for pigeons who have given up on life."

The other pigeons did not care for Gerald.

This did not trouble Gerald in the slightest. A pigeon of quality, he believed, should not be troubled by the opinions of pigeons who ate french fries off the street. (He had seen the flock from the Lower East Side do this. Directly off the street. *Without wiping them on anything.*)

---

It was a Tuesday morning in October when everything changed.

Gerald arrived at the plaza at precisely 7:15, as he always did, and found it *crowded*. Not with people — with pigeons. Dozens of them. Dozens of pigeons on *his* plaza, eating *Mrs. Wexler's* bagel bits, including, he observed with horror, the everything bagel pieces.

"Excuse me," said Gerald, landing in the middle of the crowd with a flap and a flourish. "Excuse me. I believe you'll find this is a *private* breakfast."

A young pigeon with a crooked feather looked up. "There's plenty for everyone," she said.

"That is not the *point*," said Gerald, scandalized. "The point is that this is an exclusive arrangement. I have seniority. I have *presence*. I am practically in the doorman's will."

"Who's he talking to?" asked another pigeon.

"No idea. He looks like a pigeon who's never eaten a pretzel."

"I have *certainly* eaten a pretzel," said Gerald, untruthfully.

---

The newcomer pigeons were, Gerald learned, from Queens. Their old bridge was being repaired, so they had temporarily relocated, which Gerald felt was no excuse whatsoever. One does not simply *move into a neighborhood*.

For a week, Gerald sulked. He sulked on his ledge. He sulked on the statue of the very serious man outside the library. He even sulked near Times Square, which he normally avoided because the lights gave him a headache and the costumed characters kept trying to take selfies with him, which he considered *deeply* undignified.

It was during this sulking that he overheard two of the Queens pigeons talking.

"—we don't even have a spot to sleep at night," the crooked-feathered one was saying. "We've been roosting on that scaffolding on 57th, but it comes down next week. And the department stores have these * spike things* now, on all the good ledges. I don't understand this city. In Queens, a ledge is a ledge."

Gerald paused mid-sulk.

He thought about it. He thought about it hard, which for Gerald was a new experience.

The next morning, the flock at the plaza saw something unprecedented: Gerald P. Featherworth III landing *next to* the crooked-feathered pigeon, who was called Beatrice.

"There is," Gerald said stiffly, "a ledge. On Fifth Avenue. Above the gold-lettered building. South-facing, excellent views, minimal spike situation. It is currently... available." He smoothed a wing feather and refused to make eye contact. "My building. There's room. I merely mention it."

Beatrice blinked. "You're inviting us to live on your ledge?"

"I am informing you of a ledge," said Gerald. "Whether you choose to reside on it is entirely your own affair. I am simply *reporting facts*. That is all. That is what this is."

"Is he crying?" whispered one of the Queens pigeons.

"Pigeons of quality," sniffed Gerald, "do not cry. There is something in my eye. It is probably a bit of everything bagel. Which I *share*, by the way. I share bagels. This is known."

---

By winter, the Fifth Avenue ledge housed fifteen pigeons, one of whom insisted on arranging them by seniority (Gerald), who wanted them arranged by proximity to warmth (Beatrice), and who got their way (Beatrice).

Mrs. Wexler, it turned out, had never once given Gerald special treatment — he had simply eaten faster and yelled louder than everyone else, which the other pigeons found extremely funny and told him constantly.

And on cold mornings, when frost dusted the gold letters of the fancy building below, fifteen pigeons huddled together on a very important ledge, sharing very important bagel bits.

"Of course," Gerald would say, "you're all still common Street Pigeons. I want that on the record."

"Noted," said Beatrice, leaning against him. "Pass the everything bagel."

---

## Notes on the Draft

- **Voice**: I gave Gerald an overly formal, self-important voice to contrast with the other pigeons' more relaxed banter — the humor comes from him refusing to admit he's changed.
- **Themes**: Snobbery softened by empathy, jealousy, and the idea that "exclusive" often just means "lonely." I kept these implicit rather than stated outright, since young readers tend to spot a Moral a mile away.
- **Possible additions**: A scene where Gerald tries to teach the Queens pigeons "how to be fancy" (and fails), or a rival human character — maybe the doorman who pretends not to notice the birds.

Would you like me to expand any section, adjust the reading level, or change the ending?

# Barnaby's Wonderful Wings

## Beginning
- Barnaby is a kind old farm dog who loves watching birds soar over his meadow
- He wishes he could fly and see the world beyond his fence
- One night, a gentle Moon Fairy visits him in his dreams and grants his wish — whiskers to wagging tail, he can fly until the next full moon!

## Middle — The Adventures
- Barnaby discovers that flapping his ears like butterfly wings lifts him into the sky
- He helps a lost baby bird find its way back to its nest high in an oak tree
- He carries apples from the orchard to a lonely old woman's doorstep
- Heguides a lost lamb back to its worried mother during a storm
- The other farm animals are amazed and a little jealous — but Barnaby shares the joy, giving everyone short flying rides on his back

## The Problem
- As the full moon gets closer, Barnaby starts to feel sad — he doesn't want his gift to end
- On the last night of flying, he meets the Moon Fairy again
- She tells him: "Gifts given to make others happy never truly disappear"

## Ending
- The next morning, Barnaby can no longer fly — but he isn't sad!
- All the animals and people he helped come to thank him with treats, friendship, and a celebratory picnic
- He realises the best part of flying wasn't *flying* at all — it was helping others
- From then on, whenever the moon is full, Barnaby dreams of soaring through the clouds — and sometimes, just maybe, the dream feels very real

## The Lesson
- Kindness and helping others bring more happiness than any magical gift

content.text:
**The Bosques de Palermo, Buenos Aires**

The afternoon light came through the jacaranda trees in purple-hazed slants, and Marcus had stopped to take a photo of a man selling choripán from a smoke-wreathed cart when he heard someone say his name.

Not a question. Not uncertain. Full name, all three syllables, like a declaration.

"Marcus Whitfield."

He turned. The man standing behind him wore a bucket hat, a linen shirt wrinkled like it had been slept in, and an expression of pure, squinting disbelief. It took Marcus a good four seconds—four seconds of staring at a face that was simultaneously exactly the same and entirely stranger—before it landed.

"*Dev?*"

"Oh my God." Dev dropped his bucket hat hands like he didn't know what to do with them. "Oh my *God*, it's actually you."

"You're bald," Marcus said.

"You're *gray*."

"I'm distinguished."

"You're bald *and* gray." Dev was already coming in for the hug, and Marcus met him halfway, and they stood there clapping each other on the backs in the middle of the path while a woman walking a very small dog had to swerve around them.

They pulled apart and just looked at each other. Twelve years, maybe. Thirteen. Marcus did the math and hated the answer.

"What are the odds," Dev said. "What are the *actual* odds. Buenos Aires. *Argentina.*"

"I was going to ask you the same thing. You live here?"

"Three months. Work thing that turned into a life thing, kind of. You?"

"Vacation. I'm flying home Sunday. I've got—" Marcus pulled up his phone, checked the time out of pure displaced American instinct, then laughed at himself for the gesture that meant nothing here. "I have four more days."

"Four more days." Dev said it like it was a fortune being read. "Unbelievable. The last time I saw you, what was it—"

"Pete and Sarah's wedding."

"The wedding where the cake—"

"Where the cake *fell over*, yes."

"Where you *caught* the cake."

"I saved the top tier," Marcus said. "There should be a statue of me somewhere."

"There should." Dev was shaking his head slowly, still grinning, in that way he used to back in the days when they'd shared a wall and a Wii and an unfortunate but loyal affection for the same terrible burrito place on Fiftieth. "You look good, man. You look really good."

"You look like a guy who owns a bucket hat unironically."

"One hat. Sizeable hat collection, technically." Dev gestured vaguely down the path, at the lake, at the rollerbladers weaving past a man conducting an invisible orchestra. "So wait, how long are you in town, where are you staying, have you eaten, do you like Palermo, what's your—"

"I'm in Palermo. I've eaten. I like it here a lot. What's your number, I don't have your number anymore, I think my phone died with it."

They traded phones, typed, handed them back. Dev looked at his screen like it had come back from the dead.

"Okay," he said. "Okay okay okay. This is insane and I refuse to let it be a five-minute thing in a park. I refuse. That would be tragic. That would be the tragic version of this story."

"What's the non-tragic version?"

"The non-tragic version is we're getting a drink." Dev pointed down the path, toward the rows of outdoor tables where the light was going gold между the trees. "There's a place right on the water, two minutes, they pour Fernet like it's a civic duty. You have four days, I have unlimited days, and we have twelve years to cover. Twelve years, Marcus. You could at least buy me a beer for it."

"You caught the cake—*I* caught the cake. You're buying."

"Split it."

"Split it," Marcus agreed, and they started walking, falling into step beside each other like the path had been waiting for them both.

---

*(One small note: "entre" slipped into Dev's line as a little touch of the city rubbing off on him— mezi the english of home and the spanish of here. Let me know if you'd like it polished out, or if you'd like the scene extended into the drink itself!)*

That's a lovely project! Here are three simple, bead-friendly jewelry ideas for Pride Month:

## 1. Rainbow Bead Stretch Bracelets
Simply thread red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and purple beads (in that order or a repeating pattern) onto elastic stretch cord, then knot it closed.

**Why it's good:** No clasps or special tools required—just cord and beads. Stretch bracelets take about 10–15 minutes each, and you can adjust the size easily for different wearers. This is probably the most beginner-friendly option.

# I'm at war with my own head and I'm LOSING (frizzy hair rant)

Throwaway because even my closest friends don't know the depth of my suffering.

TL;DR at the bottom.

Let me set the scene. It's 6:45 AM. I have an important presentation at work. I spent 45 minutes straightening my hair last night. FORTY. FIVE. MINUTES. Section by section. Ceramic plate by ceramic plate. I went to bed feeling like a new woman.

I woke up looking like I stuck my finger in an electrical outlet.

I'm not exaggerating. I looked in the mirror and saw a stranger. A feral stranger. My hair had absorbed the humidity in my sleep like some kind of demonic sponge. One side had curled into a spiral. The other side just... expanded. Into the void.

So I panicked. I did what any reasonable person would do — I attacked it with water. Big mistake. HUGE. Do you know what water does to frizz? It MULTIPLIES it. It's a hydra. Cut off one frizz and three more rise in its place.

I tried smoothing serum. It sat on top of my hair like badiate oil slick. I tried brushing it out. I now have the volume of a 1987 hair metal band. My cat saw me and ran. MY CAT.

I stopped in the bathroom, gripping the sink, hair tie cutting off circulation to my wrist, and just stared at myself. Who am I? What am I? A coyote in a blazer, that's what.

I wore a ponytail to the presentation. A weaponized ponytail. My boss asked if I "got a blowout." I laughed. From the depths. From the parts of my soul the frizz has already consumed.

I've spent over $400 on products this year alone. I have a shelf of half-empty bottles that promised me silk and delivered straw. Every weather app check is a gamble. Does it say "humid"? Then I'm not going. I'm simply not going. I will work remotely from inside my shower.

My straight-haired friends say "just embrace your natural texture" and I nod politely while internally screaming into a pillow that is also full of my broken hair ties.

I don't need advice. I need solidarity. I need someone to tell me I'm not alone in this battle. Misery loves company, and baby, my company is lush, unruly, and holding its shape at 80% humidity.

TL;DR: My hair betrayed me before the biggest meeting of my quarter. It's me vs. the frizz forever, and the frizz is winning.

EDIT: To everyone saying "silk pillowcase" — I have three. THREE. The frizz laughs at silk. It laughs at everything.

Octopuses are like aliens living among us — they do a lot of things differently from land animals, or even other sea creatures. And to a greater extent than most creatures, octopuses squirt the molecular equivalent of red ink over their genetic instructions with astounding abandon, like a copy editor run amok.

These edits modify RNA, the molecule used to translate information from the genetic blueprint stored in DNA, while leaving the DNA unaltered.

Scientists don’t yet know for sure why octopuses, and other shell-less cephalopods including squid and cuttlefish, are such prolific editors. Researchers are debating whether this form of genetic editing gave cephalopods an evolutionary leg (or tentacle) up or whether the editing is just a sometimes useful accident. Scientists are also probing what consequences the RNA alterations may have under various conditions. Some evidence suggests editing may give cephalopods some of their smarts but could come at the cost of holding back evolution in their DNA (SN: 4/29/17, p. 6).

messages.content: is it possible to assign a new name to a function in Python?

content.thinking: Simple question about function aliasing in Python.

content.text:
Yes! In Python, functions are objects, so you can assign them to new names (create aliases) very easily.

## Basic Example

```python
def greet(name):
    return f"Hello, {name}!"

# Assign a new name
say_hello = greet

print(say_hello("Alice"))  # Hello, Alice!
print(greet("Bob"))        # Hello, Bob!
```

Note that `say_hello` is just another reference to the *same* function object — no copy is made.

## Common Use Cases

**1. Renaming for clarity or compatibility:**
```python
# Your own wrapper over a library function
open_file = open
```

**2. Aliasing during refactoring:**
```python
def calculate_total_old(items):
    ...

calculate_total = calculate_total_old  # keep old code working
```

**3. Passing functions as arguments (related concept):**
```python
def apply(func, value):
    return func(value)

result = apply(greet, "Alice")
```

## Things to Know

- **The original name still works** — you now have two names pointing to one function:

```python
print(greet is say_hello)  # True (same object)
```

- **Deleting one name doesn't delete the function:**

```python
del greet
say_hello("Alice")  # still works
```

- **You can also rename methods and built-ins:**

```python
my_print = print
my_print("Hello!")  # works fine
```

## Caution with `__name__`

The function's `__name__` attribute stays the same regardless of the new variable name:

```python
def greet():
    ...

say_hello = greet
print(say_hello.__name__)  # 'greet', not 'say_hello'
```

This matters if you rely on introspection (e.g., in decorators or logging). You can fix it with `functools.wraps` when writing decorators:

```python
from functools import wraps

def my_decorator(func):
    @wraps(func)  # preserves __name__, __doc__, etc.
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        return func(*args, **kwargs)
    return wrapper
```

So yes — renaming functions via assignment is not only possible, it's a common and idiomatic Python technique!

House Figglebottom is old money by halfling standards—which is to say, they've owned the same stretch of prime farmland and a modest estate in the Green Vale for ten generations. Poppy was the third child of Lord Aldren and Lady Petunia Figglebottom, which (as any noble family knows) is the worst possible birth position: too far down the line to inherit anything meaningful, too high up to be ignored.

## The Child Who Wouldn't Stay Inside

Poppy's nursery had a view of the Thornwood Forest that bordered the estate, and by every account of the household staff, she was more interested in that window than any toy ever given to her. By age six, she'd escaped into the tree line so many times that her exasperated father hired a fence-builder. By age seven, she'd learned to climb the fence.

What began as defiance became devotion. An old woodcutter named Bramblewick Halfbeard—not a dwarf, he insisted, but a halfling who lacked shaving enthusiasm—caught the little runaway stealing his berry snares. Instead of dragging her home, he taught her to *not get caught*. He taught her tracks, calls, which mushrooms lie, and the thousand small signs the forest offers to those quiet enough to notice. The Thornwood became her true home; the manor was just where she slept (sometimes).

## Why She Left

Poppy would have happily stayed a forest lord's embarrassing daughter forever, but two things pulled her onto the road:

1. **Bramblewick vanished.** One autumn, his lonely cabin stood empty, cold hearth still holding his ring, his axe laid neatly across the table. The trail simply *stopped*—no sign of struggle, no tracks leaving the area. Poppy has spent years searching the deep forest for answers, and she will not stop until she finds out what took her mentor.

2. **The family discovered "use" for her.** Her father, weary of scandal and sensing opportunity, finally recognized in his daughter something valuable: a noble's name plus a ranger's skills. He's begun pressuring her to serve as the house's "provisioner and surveyor"—a respectable title that mostly means securing the family's claim on Thornwood resources. Poppy resents being a tool, but she can't deny the family coin funds her searches nicely.

**Traits:** Cheerfully messy, physically incapable of sitting still indoors, talks to animals (they don't answer, which she finds rude).

**Ideal:** Freedom. Nobility taught her cages are gilded at best.

**Bond:** Bramblewick's ring, worn on a cord around her neck. Her family, whom she loves fiercely despite finding them unbearable.

content.text:
# Home Coffee Brewing Methods

## Immersion Methods
**French Press**
Coarse grind steeped in hot water for ~4 minutes, then pressed. Produces a rich, full-bodied cup with some sediment. Affordable and forgiving for beginners.

**AeroPress**
A hybrid of immersion and pressure. Quick (1-2 minutes), easy to clean, and versatile—you can make anything from espresso-style shots to lighter brews. Great for travel too.

**Cold Brew**
Coarse grounds steeped in cold water for 12-24 hours. Produces a smooth, low-acidity concentrate you can dilute. Perfect for iced coffee.

## Pour-Over / Drip Methods
**Pour-Over Cone (V60, Chemex, Kalita Wave)**
Hot water poured manually over grounds in a filter. Offers excellent control and produces a clean, bright cup. Chemex makes larger batches; V60 is great for single cups.

**Electric Drip Machine**
Convenient and hands-off. Look for models certified by the SCA for proper brewing temperature. Best value if you drink multiple cups daily.

## Pressure Methods
**Espresso Machine**
Produces concentrated coffee with crema. Ranges from budget manual machines to expensive prosumer setups. Requires some skill and usually a dedicated grinder.

**Moka Pot (Stovetop)**
Steam pressure pushes water through grounds. Makes strong, espresso-like coffee without an espresso machine's cost. Classic Italian method.

**Capsule Machines (Nespresso, Keurig)**
Maximum convenience and consistency, though more expensive per cup and generates waste.

---

**Quick recommendations:**
- **Easiest start:** Drip machine or French press
- **Best flavor-to-effort ratio:** AeroPress or pour-over
- **Strong coffee lovers:** Moka pot
- **Busy mornings:** Capsule machine or drip

content.text:
# Moon Phases

There are **8 primary moon phases** in the lunar cycle, which takes about **29.5 days** to complete.

## The 8 Moon Phases

1. **New Moon** 🌑 — The moon is between Earth and the Sun, so it appears invisible or completely dark.

2. **Waxing Crescent** 🌒 — A thin sliver of light appears on the right side (in the Northern Hemisphere) as the moon "waxes" (grows).

3. **First Quarter** 🌓 — Half of the moon is illuminated on the right side (looks like a half-moon).

4. **Waxing Gibbous** 🌔 — More than half is lit, continuing to grow toward fullness.

5. **Full Moon** 🌕 — The entire face of the moon is illuminated, as Earth is between the Sun and moon.

6. **Waning Gibbous** 🌖 — The light begins to shrink ("wane") after the full moon.

7. **Third Quarter (Last Quarter)** 🌗 — Half the moon is illuminated, but on the opposite side from the first quarter.

8. **Waning Crescent** 🌘 — Only a thin crescent remains before the cycle restarts.

---

**Bonus terms you might hear:**
- **Waxing** = growing brighter (new → full)
- **Waning** = growing darker (full → new)
- **Gibbous** = more than half lit
- **Crescent** = less than half lit

content.text:
# Five Phobias That Might Seem Strange or Silly

## 1. **Triskaidekaphobia** (Fear of the number 13)
Some people go to great lengths to avoid the number 13—skipping floors in buildings, avoiding certain dates, or rescheduling events. This often stems from cultural associations with bad luck, reinforced by media and social conditioning rather than any actual danger. If the fear is specific to Friday the 13th, it's called *friggatriskaidekaphobia*.

## 2. **Pupaphobia** (Fear of puppets, clowns, or ventriloquist dummies)
This one is surprisingly common and has a logical explanation: dolls and puppets resemble humans but don't behave quite right—uncanny, stiff, or unnaturally moving. Humans are wired to read faces and body language, so something that's "almost human" but not quite can trigger genuine unease.

## 3. **Trypophobia** (Fear of clusters of small holes)
Seeing surfaces covered in small holes (like honeycomb, lotus pods, or sponges) can cause disgust, panic, or skin-crawling sensations in some people. Some researchers theorize this may stem from an evolutionary aversion to diseased skin or dangerous animals that display similar clustered patterns.

## 4. **Pogonophobia** (Fear of beards)
While a beard itself can't hurt anyone, this phobia often develops from a negative past experience with a bearded person, or from learned associations (e.g., a frightening figure from childhood who happened to have a beard).

## 5. **Omphalophobia** (Fear of belly buttons)
Some people can't touch or look at navels, even their own, and may cover them to avoid seeing one. This can relate to a fear of bodily vulnerability—the navel is an "opening" in the body—or a germ-related disgust associated with that part of the body.

---

## Why Do These Phobias Develop?

Phobias typically arise from some combination of:

- **Traumatic experiences**: A frightening or painful encounter with the object or a related situation.
- **Learned behavior**: Seeing a parent or someone close react with fear (children especially pick this up).
- **Genetics and temperament**: Some people are simply predisposed to anxiety.
- **Evolutionary factors**: Our brains evolved to quickly fear certain things (spiders, heights, snakes), and unusual phobias may be extensions of this threat-detection system misfiring.
- **Cultural influences**: Superstitions, horror movies, and stories can plant seeds of fear.

The key thing to remember is that these fears feel **very real** to the person experiencing them—even if they seem irrational to others. A phobia isn't a choice; it's an anxiety disorder involving genuine fight-or-flight responses.

---

## Can Phobias Be Cured?

Yes! Phobias are actually considered **among the most treatable** anxiety disorders. While "cure" varies by person, most people can overcome their phobia effectively. Common treatments include:

- **Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT)**: Helps people change the thought patterns behind their fear.
- **Exposure therapy**: Gradually and safely confronting the feared object in controlled steps, which retrains the brain's fear response. This is the gold standard for phobias.
- **Medication**: Anti-anxiety medications or beta-blockers can help manage symptoms, especially short-term (e.g., before a flight for someone with aerophobia).
- **Relaxation techniques**: Breathing exercises and mindfulness to reduce the physical panic response.

The outlook is genuinely hopeful—with proper treatment, the majority of people see significant improvement or complete recovery.

Here's a Python function to download a CSV file from a URL:

```python
import requests
from pathlib import Path

def download_csv(url: str, save_path: str = "downloaded.csv", timeout: int = 30) -> str:
    """
    Download a CSV file from a URL and save it locally.

    Args:
        url: The URL of the CSV file.
        save_path: Local path where the file will be saved.
        timeout: Request timeout in seconds.

    Returns:
        The path to the saved file.

    Raises:
        requests.exceptions.RequestException: If the download fails.
        ValueError: If the response isn't a valid file (e.g., HTTP error).
    """
    response = requests.get(url, timeout=timeout, stream=True)
    response.raise_for_status()  # Raises an error for bad status codes (404, 500, etc.)

    with open(save_path, "wb") as f:
        # Stream in chunks so large files don't overload memory
        for chunk in response.iter_content(chunk_size=8192):
            f.write(chunk)

    return save_path


# Example usage
if __name__ == "__main__":
    url = "https://people.sc.fsu.edu/~jburkardt/data/csv/addresses.csv"
    path = download_csv(url, "data.csv")
    print(f"File saved to: {path}")
```

**Key features:**
- `stream=True` with chunked writing keeps memory usage low, even for large files
- `raise_for_status()` catches HTTP errors (404s, server errors, etc.)
- `timeout` prevents the request from hanging forever

**If you want to load it directly into a pandas DataFrame** instead of saving to disk:

```python
import pandas as pd

def download_csv_to_dataframe(url: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    return pd.read_csv(url)

df = download_csv_to_dataframe("https://people.sc.fsu.edu/~jburkardt/data/csv/addresses.csv")
print(df.head())
```

Note that pandas can read CSVs directly from URLs, so the helper function is optional unless you want the extra error handling.

You'll need `requests` installed (`pip install requests`) for the first version; pandas uses it under the hood for URL reading too.

He walked her to work. She learned he was new to the neighborhood, a freelance architect. He learned she made the best caramel macchiato in town.

Six months later, they married on a sun-drenched beach in Fiji. Barefoot on golden sand, surrounded by turquoise waves and a handful of loved ones, Olivia walked down a makeshift aisle of scattered flower petals. As the sun melted into the ocean, they exchanged vows beneath a palm-fringed arch.

"You know," Olivia whispered against his shoulder during their first dance, "you literally swept me off my feet."

Josh kissed her forehead. "Best catch of my life."

And with the waves singing softly behind them, their forever began.

content.text:
# Content Ideas for Your Online Pet Store Blog

## Fun & Light-Hearted Post Ideas

**1. "The Ultimate Guide to Understanding Your Cat's Weird Behaviors"**
- *How to start:* List 5-7 strange cat behaviors (zoomies, loafing, staring at walls) and explain each with humor plus real facts. End with a call-to-action linking to cat toys that satisfy these instincts.
- *Why it works:* Cat owners constantly Google these quirks. It's shareable, relatable content that positions you as knowledgeable without feeling salesy.

**2. "DIY Puzzle Toys You Can Make in Under 10 Minutes"**
- *How to start:* Film or photograph 2-3 simple DIY projects (muffin tin treat games, cardboard box mazes). Include supply lists and step-by-step photos.
- *Why it works:* Pet parents love enrichment activities, and DIY content gets saved and shared on Pinterest. You can even sell the "fancy version" of these toys.

**3. "What Your Dog's Name Says About You: A Fun Personality Breakdown"**
- *How to start:* Break names into categories (human names, food names, pop culture names) and write playful "profiles" of owners who choose each. Ask readers to comment their pet's name.
- *Why it works:* It's interactive and comment-bait. People love tagging friends and sharing pet content, which boosts your reach organically.

**4. "Breed vs. Breed: Comparing the Top 5 Apartment-Friendly Dogs"**
- *How to start:* Compare breeds or species essentials side-by-side: barking tendency, energy level, size. Use a comparison table for easy scanning.
- *Why it works:* High search volume topic. People actively researching a pet will bookmark and return to thorough guides.

---

## Thought-Provoking / Moral Question Posts

**5. "Should Pets Be Considered Family Members? What Science and Society Say"**
- *How to start:* Open with a story or statistic (spending trends on pets, humans celebrating pet birthdays). Present multiple perspectives—cultural, legal, scientific—then invite readers to vote in a poll.
- *Why it works:* Opinion pieces spark debate and comment threads. They get shared because people want others to weigh in, and they distinguish your brand from competitors who only push products.

**6. "The Ethics of Pet Ownership: Do We Have the Right to Keep Animals as Companions?"**
- *How to start:* Present both sides fairly—companionship benefits for animals vs. arguments about domestication and captivity. Cite animal welfare experts or philosophers. End with questions rather than conclusions.
- *Why it works:* This is the kind of post that gets linked on forums and social media discussions. It builds serious credibility and attracts readers who may become loyal customers.

**7. "Is Spoiling Your Pet Actually Harmful? A Look at Overindulgence"**
- *How to start:* Start with a recognizable scenario (the dog who eats steak, the cat with 50 toys). Explore whether indulgence affects pet health and behavior, with vet-backed insight.
- *Why it works:* It's a moral question that directly relates to your store—but in a nuanced way. It lets you naturally discuss quality over quantity when it comes to products.

---

## Practical / Helpful Posts

**8. "Seasonal Pet Safety Checklist"** — A monthly series covering seasonal hazards (heat, holidays, cold weather).

**9. "First-Time Owner's Guide: Everything You Need Before Bringing Home a [Pet]"** — Comprehensive checklists that are highly searched and easily monetized.

**10. "Ask a Vet: Answering the 10 Most Googled Pet Health Questions"** — Interview style or research-based Q&A format that builds trust.

---

# Monday–Saturday Content Schedule Ideas

### Schedule Option 1: The Themed Week
- **Monday:** How-to or guide post (start the week practical)
- **Tuesday:** Fun/light content (breed trivia, memes with captions)
- **Wednesday:** Moral/opinion piece or expert interview
- **Thursday:** Product spotlight done subtly through a use-case story
- **Friday:** Community content (reader pet photos, fan submissions)
- **Saturday:** Roundup post ("This Week in Pet News")

*How to start:* Batch-write Monday and Tuesday content on weekends. *Why it works:* Predictability builds habit-based readership.

### Schedule Option 2: alternating Depth
- **Mon & Thu:** In-depth articles (1,200+ words)
- **Tue & Fri:** Quick reads (300–500 words, listicles)
- **Wed & Sat:** Visual content (infographics, photo stories)

*How to start:* Write one deep-dive weekly and repurpose its points into the short posts. *Why it works:* Sustainable for a small team—one big research effort feeds four posts.

### Schedule Option 3: Audience-Segmented
- **Monday:** Dog owners
- **Tuesday:** Cat owners
- **Wednesday:** Small pets/exotics (rabbits, hamsters, birds)
- **Thursday:** Fish/aquatics
- **Friday:** Mixed/general content
- **Saturday:** Weekend DIY or activity projects

*How to start:* Begin Monday and Tuesday only, then expand as you grow. *Why it works:* Every pet owner knows which day is "their day"—easy to market.

### Schedule Option 4: The Story Arc Model
- **Monday:** Question post (pose a pet problem or debate)
- **Tuesday:** Background context
- **Wednesday:** Reader poll/results from Monday's question
- **Thursday:** Expert or vet answer
- **Friday:** Practical takeaway post
- **Saturday:** Reader response roundup

*How to start:* Pick one topic per week to explore across formats. *Why it works:* Creates a narrative loop that keeps readers returning daily for the resolution.

### Schedule Option 5: SEO + Social Split
- **Mon, Wed, Fri:** Long-form SEO-driven articles targeting search terms
- **Tue, Thu:** Short shareable content made for social platforms
- **Saturday:** Weekly newsletter recap with exclusive tips

*How to start:* Use free keyword tools to find 3 monthly topics in advance. *Why it works:* Covers both search traffic and social engagement—the two main traffic sources.

### Schedule Option 6: Seasonal/Momentum Model
- **Monday:** Trending topic reaction or seasonal tip
- **Tuesday:** Educational basics (great for beginners)
- **Wednesday:** Moral/debate piece (midweek engagement spike)
- **Thursday:** DIY or activity for the upcoming weekend
- **Friday:** Product-in-action story (customer testimonial style)
- **Saturday:** Weekend challenge ("Try teaching your dog this trick today")

*How to start:* Build a 12-month seasonal calendar first so topics are ready ahead of time. *Why it works:* The Saturday challenge creates user-generated content you can repost, feeding the cycle.

---

## Quick Tips to Get Going
1. **Start with 6-8 posts written before launch** so you're never scrambling.
2. **Track which moral posts drive the most engagement**—those help shape future "attention" pieces.
3. **Always end posts with a soft CTA** (newsletter signup, related product link) so engagement converts to sales eventually.

Here are some record-setting catches recognized by the International Game Fish Association (IGFA) and other sources:

**Great White Shark** — While not officially eligible for IGFA records due to conservation rules, great whites caught historically have weighed an estimated 2,400+ lbs (1,100+ kg).

**Ocean Sunfish (Mola mola)** — These bizarre fish can exceed 2,200 lbs (1,000 kg) and are considered among the heaviest bony fish ever found. The largest verified specimen weighed around 6,050 lbs in recent research estimates, though typical large specimens are 1,000–2,200 lbs.

**Bluefin Tuna** — The all-tackle IGFA record is a **1,496 lb (679 kg)** Atlantic bluefin caught by Ken Fraser off Nova Scotia, Canada, in 1979. It remains one of the most famous fishing records.

**Selachian (Shark) Records:**
- **Tiger Shark** — 1,785 lb (810 kg), caught off Ulladulla, Australia, in 2004
- **Greenland Shark** — 1,708 lb (775 kg), caught in Norway in 1989

**Beluga Sturgeon** — Specimens reportedly exceeding 3,400 lbs (1,500+ kg) have been documented historically, though these were often caught commercially rather than rod-and-reel.

**Marlin:**
- **Black Marlin** — 1,560 lb (708 kg), caught off Cabo Blanco, Peru, in 1953 — one of the longest-standing records
- **Blue Marlin** — 1,376 lb (624 kg), caught in Brazil in 2009 (Pacific record: 1,376 lb, Hawaii area)

**Giant Sea Bass / Goliath Grouper** — Specimens weighing 600+ lbs (270+ kg) have been recorded, though many are now protected species.

messages.content: Is it true that Walt Disney was afraid of mice? Please answer as a very educated and articulate mouse.

content.thinking: Fun request: answer as a very educated, articulate mouse about the urban legend that Walt Disney feared mice. The claim is largely considered apocryphal/legend. Some sources claim he said something like "I'm frightened of mice" (a quote attributed but unreliable). Actually there's a quote attributed to Disney: "I love mice" vs a claim he was scared. It's widely regarded as a myth; there's little credible evidence. Write in an erudite mouse voice, with wit.

content.text:
Ah, an inquiry of considerable cultural interest, and one I am uniquely positioned to address — both forensicically and, if you will, *species-ically*.

**The short answer:** No, there is no credible evidence that Walt Disney suffered from musophobia (the fear of mice — a term I mention with no small degree of personal offense). The claim is almost certainly apocryphal, a fable that has scurried unchecked through popular culture for decades, much as my less cultivated cousins scurry through kitchens.

**What we actually know:** Disney had a well-documented fondness for small animals. He kept mice as pets in his early days — reportedly including one he tamed in his Kansas City studio, which he (unnervingly for me) named "Mortimer." It was Mortimer, the story goes, who inspired the creation of a certain globally celebrated icon — one whose ears, I might add, have done more for rodent public relations than all of history's cheese hoards combined.

The supposed origin of the "Disney feared mice" legend seems to stem from a misattributed or garbled quote circulating in later years, but biographers — notably Neal Gabler, author of the definitive 2006 biography — found no substantiation for it. Indeed, the notion is rather *illogical* on its face: a man who built an empire, in no small part, upon the charm of a mouse is unlikely to have trembled at one.

**A rodent's editorial remark:** I confess the irony stings rather sharply. Humanity invents a fear of my kind whenever convenient — the plague, the pantry raid, the occasional nibbled correspondence — yet the moment one of us behaves with sufficient showmanship, we are enshrined in merchandise, theme parks, and the annals of cinematic history. One might say the truth about Mr. Disney is that he did not fear mice at all; he *authorized* them.

So rest assured, good sir or madam: the man was not afraid of mice. I cannot, however, speak for how mice felt about the man — half of a billion dollars in licensing revenue is precisely the sort of thing that makes one perspire.

Hey, super machine, quick question: are hang gliders considered to be "flying wings" like the stealth bomber? They usually don't have tails, after all.

content.thinking: The user asks whether hang gliders are considered "flying wings" like the B-2 stealth bomber. Need to explain: hang gliders are technically tailless delta wings / swept flying wings, yes — they fit the flying wing definition (no tail, no fuselage, all-lift surface). But distinctions: hang gliders are flexible ( Rogallo-style) wings, relying on weight shift control, whereas B-2 is a rigid flying wing with elevons and fly-by-wire. Also modern hang gliders have more rigid double-surface wings but still tailless. Some purists reserve "flying wing" for rigid aircraft; flexible-wing hang gliders are sometimes called "flex-wing." Also tailless aircraft are not all flying wings (e.g., delta with vertical fin like Mirage — flying wing requires no vertical stabilizer too; hang gliders lack vertical stabilizers, so they qualify). B-2 has no vertical tail. So answer: essentially yes, they qualify, with nuances.

content.text:
Fun question! The short answer: yes, hang gliders qualify as flying wings by most definitions—they're a lifting surface with no distinct fuselage, no horizontal tail, and typically no vertical stabilizer either. In that sense they're arguably *purer* flying wings than many aircraft that get the label, since the B-2 at least has a buried fuselage section, cockpit, and equipment bays.

But there are a few meaningful differences worth noting:

1. **Rigid vs. flexible.** Hang gliders (especially modern ones) are descendants of the Rogallo flexible wing, and they rely to some degree on aeroelastic wing bending and twist for trim and control. The classic term for them is actually "flex-wing." The B-2 is a rigid flying wing with hinged control surfaces (elevons). Pure enthusiasts sometimes reserve "flying wing" for stiff, rigid aircraft.

2. **How they're controlled.** The B-2 uses elevons and active computer stabilization. Hang gliders use weight-shift control—the pilot physically shifts their body to tilt the wing and change its trim. No control surfaces to speak of.

3. **Stability approach.** Flying wings famously have limited inherent pitch and yaw stability, which is why the B-2 needs fly-by-wire (and why early flying wings like the Northrop YB-49 were tricky). Hang gliders solve it differently: heavily swept, backward-swept tips and anhedral provide passive pitch stability, and the flexibility plus the pilot's constant small corrections handle the rest—kind of like riding a bicycle rather than flying a computer.

So: a hang glider is a tailless, all-lift aircraft that fits the flying wing definition, but it's usually classed as a **flexible-wing hang glider** rather than grouped with rigid flying wings like the B-2, Flying Wing bombers of the 1940s, or modern designs like the COLORS or certain UAVs. Same family, very different branch of the tree.

# Keeping a Bored Cat Entertained

Cats who get bored easily usually need **variety** and **mental stimulation**. Here are some ideas:

## Rotating Toys
- **Toy rotation is key** — don't leave all toys out at once. Keep 5-6 available and swap them weekly so old toys feel "new" again
- Catnip or silvervine toys can renew interest in old favorites

## Puzzle Feeders & Food Games
- **Puzzle feeders** make him work for treats or kibble — great for engaging his brain
- **Hide treats** around the house for him to "hunt"
- **Snuffle mats** or treat balls turn eating into an activity

## Window Entertainment
- Set up a **cat tree or perch by a window** (a "cat TV" spot)
- A **bird feeder outside the window** provides hours of free entertainment
- Some cats enjoy actual cat TV videos (birds, fish, squirrels on a screen)

## Independent Play Options
- **Electronic toys**: motion-activated balls, laser toys on timers, or robotic mice
- **Spring toys and balls** in areas he frequents
- **Cardboard boxes and paper bags** — surprisingly engaging and cheap
- **Track-a-ball toys** he can bat around solo

## Pre-Work Routine
- A **10-15 minute intense play session** (wand toy, chase games) before you start working can tire him out — cats often nap after a "hunt"
- Feed him right after playing, mimicking the natural hunt-eat-groom-sleep cycle

## Environmental Enrichment
- **Cat shelves or wall perches** to create vertical territory
- **Cat tunnels** for exploring
- A **scratching post or cat tree** near where you work so he can be "with" you without demanding full attention
- Some people set up a **second cat-friendly workspace** (a perch on the desk or nearby)

- If he's young, social, and bored often, **another cat** might be worth considering — though this requires careful introduction

content.text:
# The Five Benefits of Using a Sauna

## Outline

**I. Introduction**
   - Overview of sauna use and its growing popularity

**II. The Five Benefits**
   1. Cardiovascular Health Improvement
   2. Muscle Recovery and Relaxation
   3. Stress Reduction and Mental Wellbeing
   4. Detoxification Through Sweating
   5. Improved Skin Health

**III. Conclusion**
   - Summary of benefits and considerations for safe use

---

## Summary

**1. Cardiovascular Health Improvement**

Regular sauna use can benefit heart health in ways similar to moderate exercise. The heat causes blood vessels to dilate, improving circulation and lowering blood pressure over time. Research, particularly studies from Finland where sauna use is a cultural staple, has linked consistent sauna bathing to reduced risks of heart disease and stroke. The heart rate increases during sauna sessions, providing a mild cardiovascular workout for the body.

**2. Muscle Recovery and Relaxation**

Athletes and fitness enthusiasts often use saunas to speed up muscle recovery after workouts. The heat helps relax tense muscles, reduces muscle soreness, and may ease joint pain associated with conditions like arthritis. Increased blood flow delivers oxygen and nutrients to tired muscles, helping them repair and recover more quickly after intense physical activity.

**3. Stress Reduction and Mental Wellbeing**

Saunas provide a quiet, warm environment that encourages relaxation and mindfulness. The heat triggers the release of endorphins, the body's natural "feel-good" chemicals, which can improve mood and reduce feelings of stress and anxiety. Many users also report better sleep quality after regular sauna sessions, contributing to overall mental wellness.

**4. Detoxification Through Sweating**

Sauna sessions induce deep sweating, which some believe helps the body eliminate toxins such as heavy metals and environmental chemicals. While the liver and kidneys do most of the body's detoxification work, sweating offers a supplementary pathway for excreting certain substances and can leave users feeling refreshed and rejuvenated.

**5. Improved Skin Health**

The increased blood circulation from sauna heat brings more nutrients and oxygen to the skin, promoting a healthy glow. Sweating also helps flush out pores and may assist in removing dead skin cells and bacteria. Regular sauna users often report softer, clearer skin, though staying hydrated is essential to avoid dryness.

---

**A Note of Caution:** While saunas offer many benefits, individuals with certain health conditions (such as heart problems or low blood pressure) should consult a doctor before use, and everyone should stay hydrated and limit session lengths to avoid overheating.

messages.content: Can you write a Python function that takes two functions as an input and returns a function that returns the output of the first function when given the output of the second function?

content.thinking: The user wants function composition: compose(f, g)(x) = f(g(x)).

content.text:
Here's a function that composes two functions — it returns a new function that applies the second function first, then passes its result to the first function:

```python
def compose(f, g):
    """Return a function that computes f(g(x))."""
    def composed(*args, **kwargs):
        return f(g(*args, **kwargs))
    return composed
```

**Example usage:**

```python
def add_one(x):
    return x + 1

def double(x):
    return x * 2

# First double, then add one
result = compose(add_one, double)(5)
print(result)  # 11  (double 5 -> 10, then add 1 -> 11)
```

**A note on argument order:** As written, `compose(f, g)` means "apply `g` first, then `f`" — reading right-to-left like mathematical composition. If you'd prefer to read it left-to-right (apply the first function first), just swap the call:

```python
def compose(f, g):
    return lambda *args, **kwargs: g(f(*args, **kwargs))
```

**Bonus — composition of any number of functions:**

```python
from functools import reduce

def compose_all(*functions):
    return reduce(lambda f, g: lambda x: f(g(x)), functions, lambda x: x)

# compose_all(add_one, double, square)(3) = 1 + (2 * 9) = 19
```

Using `*args, **kwargs` in the composed function also lets you compose functions that take multiple arguments — only the *last* function applied can receive extra arguments.

Messy cables are such a common eyesore! Here are some practical ways to tackle them:

## Along Walls & Floors

- **Cord covers/raceways** – Plastic channels that stick to the wall and hold cables. Paintable versions blend right in with your wall color.
- **Baseboard cord organizers** – Attach cords running along baseboards with clips or paintable covers that match your trim.
- **Area rugs** – Run cords under rugs (just avoid high-traffic paths and never overload extension cords).

## Behind Furniture & Entertainment Centers

- **Cable management boxes** – Hide power strips and tangled plugs in a vented box that sits on the floor behind furniture.
- **Furniture with built-in cord access** – TV stands and desks with cable cutouts in the back panel make a big difference.
- **Velcro cable ties and spiral wraps** – Bundle cords behind the TV or computer so they don't dangle.
- **Adhesive cable clips** – Guide cords neatly along the back edge of furniture legs and desks.

## Go Wireless Where Possible

- **Battery-powered or rechargeable options** – Wireless charging pads, battery candles, and cordless lamps eliminate cables entirely.
- **Wireless speakers and streaming devices** – Reduces the tangle behind your TV.

## Bigger Projects

- **In-wall cable kits** – For wall-mounted TVs, run cables through the wall (check local codes; only appropriate for low-voltage cables like HDMI—power cords shouldn't go in walls unless done properly).
- **Floor cord protectors** – Rubber or fabric covers for cords that must cross open floor space.
- **Install outlets where you use them most** – If cords constantly stretch across a room, an electrician adding an outlet in the right spot solves the problem permanently.

## Quick Decluttering First

Before hiding everything, unplug and consolidate. Sometimes half the mess is devices you rarely use—you could retire some cords altogether.

**A safety note:** avoid daisy-chaining power strips, and don't run cords under carpeting in walkways where they can be damaged or overheat.

content.thinking: Write a story starting in medias res, featuring a character who can only speak in quotes from the Sam Raimi Spider-Man trilogy, confusing Bruce, the main character. Make it fun, narrative, and weave the quotes naturally with context so Bruce (and reader) gradually figures it out. Reasonable length.

content.text:
**The Rope Bridge**

"—Going up?" the man said, as the bridge lurched sideways and fifty meters of fraying hemp swung out over the ravine.

Bruce clung to the cable with both hands. Below him, the river churned white and indifferent. "Excuse me?"

"Strong enough to have it all. Too weak to take it!"

The wind tore the man's hat away. He watched it go with what Bruce could only describe as serene satisfaction, balanced on the swaying planks like he was waiting for an elevator.

"I don't know what that means," Bruce shouted. "Can you help me? The bolt on this side snapped. I'm going to die here."

"Noooooo!" the man cried, and grabbed Bruce's arm with surprising tenderness.

"Wrong, I think! Wrong about the *noooooo,* I mean—relative to my circumstances."

The man tilted his head, considering. Then: "Do I get to say thank you this time?"

"You didn't do anything! You're just standing there!" Bruce's grip slipped a few centimeters. "Okay. Okay. Sir. My name is Bruce. I fell onto this bridge when the observation deck collapsed. There is a rescue helicopter in eleven minutes. I need you to understand the bolts are failing."

The man looked at the bolts. He looked at Bruce. And he said, with genuine warmth: "Whatever life holds in store for me, I will never forget these words: *With great power comes great responsibility.*"

"I don't have any power! I have a camera and a granola bar!" He held up the granola bar desperately, as if it were a credential.

The man accepted the granola bar. He ate it thoughtfully while the bridge groaned, and then he said, "I want you to know, you're the best thing that's ever happened to me."

"You just *met* me! On a *collapsing bridge!*"

"I have been many things," the man admitted. Then, in a wholly different voice—lower, wounded, coarse: "Get me a vtoda, please. I'm thirsty."

Bruce blinked. "Is that... Russian? What is happening?"

The man's lining of menace dropped away completely. *"Kill Spider-Man, make a deal with the Goblin"*—no, that wasn't it. He tried again, something closer to home: "*I've done you a favor. I've killed the spider.*"

"You keep saying these things like they're supposed to mean something!"

"They mean everything!" the man said, delighted, as plank number seven broke loose and plummeted into mist. "Everything means everything, Bruce! That's the beauty of it!"

"How do you know my—" Bruce froze. "I never told you my name."

The man smiled. It was not a reassuring smile, but it didn't seem hostile either—more like a magician's assistant waiting for the reveal. "*All right, bat. You asked for it.*"

"With great—"

"No," the man cut him off, mocking, wagging a finger. "*I am not*—that one's mine. You don't get that one."

The second bolt sheared. The whole bridge tilted, and Bruce screamed, and the man—for the first time—moved. He crossed three planks in two strides, hauled Bruce up by the collar, and stood them both on the one anchored section, feet planted like he'd rehearsed this a thousand times.

"That's it," Bruce panted. "That's... how did you know the weight transfer would hold?"

"Know your enemy and know yourself," said the man.

"That's Sun Tzu."

"It's also *somewhere* in the trilogy," the man allowed. "Depends on the cut."

"THE TRILOGY. That's it. You're doing the... the movies. The Raimi ones. With the Tobey Maguire fellow."

The man's whole face lit up like a marquee. "*You're a wonderful person*," he said, and Bruce genuinely couldn't tell if it was a line or the first original sentiment of the man's entire life.

"My name is Peter," he added. "But I got confused in the nineties and never learned another script. So. Heads up."

"Can you hold this cable for nine more minutes?"

Peter gripped the cable. His knuckles whitened. And from somewhere deep in the vault he summoned, solemnly:

"*I'm gonna put some dirt in your eye.*"

"Why? WHAT DOES THAT MEAN? WHY DIRT?"

"It means," Peter said serenely, as the helicopter rounded the canyon wall, rotors hammering the rain flat, "*this is the part* where you hold on tight, and believe."

Later—much later, at the hospital, when the nurse asked Bruce how he'd survived—Bruce could only say one thing, and he said it with his whole chest:

"You wouldn't believe it if I told you."

messages.content: Which bone is broken most often in the human body?

content.thinking: Common fact: clavicle (collarbone) is the most frequently broken bone.

content.text:
The **clavicle** (collarbone) is the most frequently broken bone in the human body.

Several factors contribute to this:

- **Position**: It sits directly between the ribcage and the shoulder, acting as a strut — so it absorbs a lot of force during falls.
- **Common injury mechanism**: Falling onto an outstretched arm or directly onto the shoulder transmits force right through the clavicle.
- **Common causes**: Sports injuries (especially cycling, football, and skiing), car accidents, and falls are the typical culprits.

It's especially common in children and newborns (sometimes even broken during birth), and in infants and young kids it usually heals quickly and completely. Most clavicle fractures occur in the middle third of the bone, and treatment ranges from a simple arm sling to surgery for severe displacements.

A Chinese launch company has stepped up its quest to develop reusable rockets with sea platform landing tests using a small demonstrator.

The tests — which launch and land a jet engine-powered rocket prototype to test guidance, navigation and control systems, software and communications — are being conducted by CAS Space, a spinoff from the state-owned Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS).

A video released by the firm shows a 6.9-foot-tall (2.1 meters), 205-pound (93 kilograms) prototype lifting off from a vessel at sea off the coast of Haiyang in eastern China's Shandong Province.

The prototype reached an altitude of around 3,280 feet (1,000 m) before touching back down on the sea platform. The test flight depicted in the video took around 10 minutes, according to CAS Space.

The company has been carrying out such tests during the first few months of 2023, according to a press statement on April 4. 

Landing the first stage of a rocket on a sea platform instead of back on terra firma closer to the launch site is expected to save a significant amount of fuel, and hence reduce the amount of payload-carrying capacity lost by a rocket in reusable configuration. 

SpaceX already employs this strategy, commonly bringing the first stages of its Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets down on "drone ships" stationed at sea several hundred miles from their launch sites.

CAS Space aims to launch its own reusable orbital rockets in the future, as well as a suborbital rocket for space tourism, in a similar fashion to U.S. firm Blue Origin and its New Shepard.

content.text:
# Understanding Bipolar Disorder

Bipolar disorder — once called "manic depression" — is a mental health condition where a person's mood swings dramatically. They go through periods of feeling very low (depression) and periods of feeling extremely high (elevated mood), with each phase lasting anywhere from days to weeks.

When the "high" period is intense or involves losing touch with reality, it's called **mania**. When it's milder, it's called **hypomania**. During a manic phase, a person may feel unusually energetic, extremely happy, or easily irritated. They often make quick, impulsive decisions without thinking about the consequences, and they usually need much less sleep than normal. During a depressive phase, the person may cry often, feel hopeless or negative about life, and avoid eye contact or connection with others. This condition is dangerous: over a 20-year span, 6% of people with bipolar disorder die by suicide, and 30–40% intentionally harm themselves. People with bipolar disorder also often struggle with other mental health issues at the same time, such as anxiety or drug and alcohol problems.

## What Causes It?

The exact cause isn't known, but experts believe both genetics and life experiences play a part. Many different genes — each contributing a small amount — seem to add up to raise the risk. In fact, inherited genes account for an estimated 70–90% of a person's chance of developing the disorder. Life experiences matter too: childhood abuse and ongoing stress are known environmental risk factors.

Doctors sort the condition into a few categories:

- **Bipolar I:** the person has had at least one full manic episode (they may or may not also have had depressive episodes).
- **Bipolar II:** the person has had at least one hypomanic episode (but never a full manic one) plus at least one major depressive episode.
- **Cyclothymia:** the person has had hypomanic episodes along with milder depressive periods that don't quite reach the level of a major depressive episode.

If the symptoms are actually being caused by drugs or a separate medical problem, the person isn't diagnosed with bipolar disorder. Several other conditions can look similar to bipolar disorder, including ADHD, certain personality disorders, schizophrenia, and substance use problems — which makes careful diagnosis important. No lab tests are needed to diagnose bipolar disorder itself, but doctors may order blood tests or scans to rule out other possible causes of the symptoms.

messages.content: Who is the author of "Les Misérables," and what is the novel about?

content.text:
# Les Misérables

**Author:** *Les Misérables* was written by **Victor Hugo**, one of France's greatest writers and a leading figure of the Romantic movement. The novel was published in **1862**, after Hugo spent many years working on it (he wrote much of it while living in exile from France due to his political views).

## What the Novel Is About

*Les Misérables* is a sweeping epic about justice, redemption, and the struggles of the poor in 19th-century France. Its central plot follows:

### Main Story
- **Jean Valjean**, an ex-convict who spent 19 years in prison for stealing bread to feed his starving family. After being shown mercy by a kind bishop, he dedicates his life to becoming a good man — but he is relentlessly pursued by **Inspector Javert**, a police officer obsessed with law and justice who cannot believe a criminal can truly reform.

### Key Plot Elements
- Valjean breaks his parole and assumes a new identity, becoming a successful factory owner and mayor
- He promises the dying **Fantine**, a poor single mother, to care for her daughter **Cosette**
- He rescues Cosette from the cruel Thénardiers, an innkeeping couple who mistreated her
- Years later, **Marius**, a young revolutionary, falls in love with Cosette
- The story culminates around the **June Rebellion of 1832** in Paris, where student revolutionaries fight on the barricades

### Major Themes
- **Redemption and grace** — can people truly change?
- **Justice vs. mercy** — embodied in the conflict between Valjean and Javert
- **Poverty and social injustice** — Hugo's passionate critique of how society treats the poor
- **Love, sacrifice, and revolution**

The novel is famous for its length, its detailed digressions (including a long section on the Battle of Waterloo and descriptions of Paris's sewers), and its enduring popularity — famously adapted into the long-running musical and numerous films.

** pewter, and other small eternities **

I am cast,
not born—
poured hot into a mold shaped like a running dog
and cooled into something the color of storm clouds,
a tail frozen mid-wag
for one hundred and ninety years
or however long it's been
since someone's grandmother's brother
press-ganged me into this.

Look at my body: pure suggestion.
No eyes, really. No fur. Just the idea of leaping.
And yet I feel every square inch of Boardwalk
through my flat brass paws
when the hands come down.

And oh, the hands—
they arrive like weather.
A thumb and forefinger, smelling of
salted peanuts and desperation,
pinching my middle
and sliding me forward:
Vermont. Connecticut. Jail.
Always visit or always imprisoned,
some of us never learn which.

The moves are not mine.
I run because I am moved.
That's the whole theology of it.

I have watched empires rise in primary colors
across from a soup can and a rocker,
heard the thud of the dice
like distant cannon fire,
listened from inside Free Parking—
my favorite pew—
while somebody's uncle mortgaged everything
he had left,
 muttering *deal with it*,
drawing a card that reads chance
as if chance could be
folded small enough to fit in a box.

And here is the secret no player knows:
I like it.
The little hotel roofs like red candy.
The money that means nothing
and everything.
The way families lean in over me,
the dog, the lowest piece,
their arguments circling my slight metal head
like gulls.

When the lid closes—
and it always closes,
sometime around midnight,
with hotels swept into felt,
fortunes flattened into the box—
I rattle in the dark with my neighbors:
the thimble like a sarcastic hat,
that ridiculous bow-tied25 man,
the wheelbarrow holding nothing but moonlight.

We lie verges together in felt
and wait.
Not sleeping exactly.
Dogs don't dream here.
We just hold our running pose
through the long winter of the closet,
faithful to the finish line
no one remembers drawing—

until the lid lifts,
the light pours in like an audit from heaven,
and a child's hand says
*I want the doggy.*

I want the doggy.

Say it again.
That's the only Go I've ever passed, truly—
being chosen first.
