content.text:
The first three Presidents of the United States were:

1. **George Washington** (1789–1797) — The first president, who had previously led the Continental Army during the American Revolutionary War. He was unanimously elected by the Electoral College and set many precedents for the office, including the tradition of serving only two terms.

2. **John Adams** (1797–1801) — Washington's vice president and a key figure in the push for independence. He was a member of the Federalist Party and the only one of the first three presidents who was not a Virginian (he was from Massachusetts).

3. **Thomas Jefferson** (1801–1809) — The author of the Declaration of Independence. He was Adams's vice president, then defeated him in the election of 1800. He founded the Democratic-Republican Party and completed the Louisiana Purchase during his presidency.

# Debugging Despair

**I.**

Blank screen, cursor blinks
I type the first confident line
It will not compile

Stack trace like lightning
points where I do not dare look
the bug is not there

**III.**

One small change made
Now fourteen tests are broken
Undone, it still fails

**IV.**

Rubber duck listens
I explain my clever code
and hear my error

**V.**

Stack Overflow sighs
"This question was answered"
closed as duplicate

**VI.**

It works on my machine
I whisper the古老 lie again
It fails here as well

**VII.**

Three a.m. glow
the problem seems so simple now
why did I not see

**VIII.**

Rebuilt from nothing
line by line, patient, careful
fails the same quiet way

**IX.**

I print each value
reason through every branch, every loop
off by one, of course

**X.**

Green checkmarks cascade
The build succeeds at Brooks' dawn
I forgot why it broke

messages.content: Who is Joe Hisaishi? What is he famous for?

content.text:
# Joe Hisaishi (久石譲)

Joe Hisaishi is one of Japan's most celebrated and influential composers, born **Mamoru Fujisawa** on December 6, 1950, in Nakano, Japan. He adopted the name "Joe Hisaishi" as a pseudonym—it's playfully derived from the Japanese reading of Quincy Jones' name.

## What He's Famous For

### Studio Ghibli Collaboration
Hisaishi is best known as the longtime composer for **Hayao Miyazaki's animated films at Studio Ghibli**. His scores are inseparable from the emotional power of these beloved films, including:

- **Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind** (1984) — their first collaboration
- **My Neighbor Totoro** (1988)
- **Kikila's Delivery Service** (1989)
- **Princess Mononoke** (1997)
- **Spirited Away** (2001)
- **Howl's Moving Castle** (2004)
- **Ponyo** (2008)
- **The Wind Rises** (2013)
- **The Boy and the Heron** (2023)

The soundtrack to *Spirited Away* and the piece "One Summer's Day" are particularly iconic worldwide.

### Beyond Ghibli
- He has scored films by director **Takeshi Kitano**, including *Hana-bi* and *Brother*
- He composed music for many live-action Japanese films, such as *Departures* (2008), which won the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film

### Live Performances
Hisaishi is also renowned as a conductor and pianist. His **"Symphonic Concert: Music from the Studio Ghibli Films"** tours have sold out venues globally, bringing his film music to symphony halls around the world.

## Why He Matters
His style blends minimalism (he was influenced by composers like Philip Glass and Terry Riley), Japanese musical traditions, classical orchestration, and electronic music. His melodic, emotive scores have made him one of the most recognizable film composers in the world, often described as the "John Williams of Japan."

# The Big Game

My name is Tommy, and today is the biggest day of my whole life. It's the championship game!

I woke up before the sun even came up. My baseball glove sat on my nightstand, and I gave it a little pat, like it was a puppy. "Today's the day, Dusty," I whispered. I named my glove Dusty because that's where he lives—right in the dust of the pitcher's mound.

At breakfast, I was too nervous to eat my pancakes. They just sat there looking at me, and I looked at them. My mom ruffled my hair and said, "You've practiced all season, Tommy. Just have fun out there."

Easy for her to say. She's not the one who has to play second base in front of the *whole entire town*.

When I got to the field, kids were everywhere. Red team jerseys, blue team jerseys, popcorn, hot dogs, and that smell I love the most—fresh cut grass. Coach Ramirez gave us all a high five as we ran onto the field.

"Play hard, play fair, and smile," he said. That's his three rules.

The first inning was scary. The other team, the Rockets, hit a home run! But then our shortstop, Maria, caught a fly ball, and everybody cheered so loud my ears rang.

Then it was my turn to bat. My legs felt like spaghetti. The pitcher on the Rockets is really tall, and he looked VERY tall from all the way at home plate. I held up my bat and pulled my helmet down tight.

"One strike!" the umpire called. I swung and missed! I heard my best friend Sam yell from the dugout, "You got this, Tommy!"

I took a deep breath, just like Coach taught me. In through the nose, out through the mouth.

I gripped the bat. The pitcher wound up.

Here comes the pitch...

content.text:
That's a fun character to build! Here are some elements that could appear on his worker ID, ranging from practical to flavor-rich:

## Core Identification
- **Full name** (possibly with a corporate designation number, like "J. Vasquez-7704")
- **Photo or biometric scan** (retinal pattern, since helmets/haze can obscure faces)
- **Employee number** — often more important than the name in a corporate mining operation
- **Blood type and medical alerts** (allergies to common pipe sealants, synthetic adrenaline sensitivity, etc.)
- **Species/genetic modifications**, if your setting has gene-tweaked workers adapted for low gravity

## Occupational Details
- **Job classification** —Drill Operator, Vac-Welder, Ore Sorter, Shaft Rat, etc.
- **Certification levels** — e.g., "Class 3 EVA Certified," "Licensed Demolitions," "Pressurized Rescue Trained"
- **Issuing corporation or union local** ("Belter Workers' Collective — Local 12" gives instant class/political flavor)
- **Current assignment** — asteroid designation (like "433 Eros — Claim 88-C") or ship/station name
- **Shift designation** and habitat pod assignment

## Safety & Logistics
- **Suit size and helmet compatibility** — practical for getting gear fast in an emergency
- **Radiation exposure tally** — a cumulative dose tracker is poignant; you could show he's near his lifetime limit
- **Insurance class** — hazard pay tier, or chillingly, "Non-Recoverable Asset Clause: Yes/No"
- **Oxygen allotment code** or ration tier
- **Emergency contact** — next of kin, or "None on file" for a lone-wolf character

## Great Character-Building Details
- **Expiration date looming** — a contract nearly up creates instant tension
- **Stamps or stickers** — commendations, disciplinary marks, union dues paid
- **Wear and tear** — scratched, scorched from a near-miss, a corner melted by a plasma torch
- **A second, illegible ID** from a defunct company or dead station, kept as a keepsake

A nice touch: decide whether it's a physical chipped card, a tattooed QR code on the wrist (harder to lose when you're stripping bodies from a blown airlock), or an implant. Each choice says something different about how much his employer trusts — or surveils — him.

Want help developing the company or the setting's labor politics next? Those IDs tend to reflect the world's power structure pretty directly.

The root causes of the conflict can be traced to the crisis of 14th-century Europe. The outbreak of war was motivated by a gradual rise in tension between the kings of France and England over territory; the official pretext was the question that arose because of the interruption of the direct male line of the Capetian dynasty.

English holdings in France had varied in size, at some points dwarfing even the French royal domain; by 1337, however, only Gascony was English.
In 1328, Charles IV of France died without any sons or brothers, and a new principle, Salic law, disallowed female succession. Charles's closest male relative was his nephew Edward III of England, whose mother, Isabella, was Charles's sister. Isabella claimed the throne of France for her son by the rule of proximity of blood, but the French nobility rejected this, maintaining that Isabella could not transmit a right she did not possess. content.text:
# Susan and Tanya's Mountain Getaway

Susan the snake lay sprawled across the warm sand, fanning herself with a palm frond. "Tanya, I love the beach, but I simply cannot take another day of this heat!"

Tanya the turtle, who was nibbling on a bit of seaweed nearby, nodded knowingly. "I hear you, Susan. My shell feels like a little oven. You know what we need? A holiday!"

"A holiday!" Susan's eyes lit up. "But where? Somewhere cool, somewhere green..."

"The mountains!" Tanya declared. "My cousin Gerald went there last summer. He said the air is crisp, the streams are chilly, and the shade trees go on forever!"

The very next morning, the two friends set off together. Susan coiled herself comfortably on top of Tanya's shell.

"Free ride for you," Tanya chuckled. "That guilting snake look from the beach could at least provide something."

"I'll pay you in stories!" Susan promised, and she kept her word, spinning delightful tales as they climbed the winding trail up the mountainside.

When they finally arrived, both friends gasped. Before them stretched a sparkling stream fed by snowmelt, surrounded by towering pines that whispered in the cool breeze. Susan slithered down and onto the soft moss beneath a fern, sighing happily.

"This is paradise," she said.

Tanya waded into the shallow, icy stream and splashed around joyfully. "Cousin Gerald was right about everything!"

For days, the friends explored the mountain together. They played hide-and-seek among the wildflowers, sampled sweet mountain berries, and lay on a smooth boulder watching the clouds drift by like lazy clouds.

"This was the best idea you've ever had," Susan admitted one evening, her scales gleaming in the golden sunset light.

"Even the leaf thing?" Susan laughed. "It was silly. The breeze up here does the work for free."

They curled up together under a canopy of stars, cool and content, already planning their next trip—which would be during the winter, they decided, to somewhere sunny.

Best friends, best memories, and the perfect escape. What more could a snake and a turtle ask for?

Nora Whitfield had been staring at the same square of carpet for twenty minutes. It was a等服务—she corrected herself, a *loophole* in the hotel carpet, a pale seam where the housekeepers' vacuum never quite reached, and she had memorized it completely rather than do the one thing she needed to do: walk downstairs.

Below her, through the floor, she could feel it—the low rumble of the partisan crowd in Marlowe's, the restaurant that occupied the hotel's ground floor. Her people. Dee was down there, probably pacing near the bar in the green dress she'd promised was "lucky," though nothing about this night had been lucky so far. Priya was down there refreshing five feeds at once. Her brother Tom was down there, telling his story about the paper route and eight-year-old Nora delivering news before she could even vote, which he told at every gathering, and which she pretended to hate.

Four hundred and eleven votes. That was her margin when she'd come upstairs an hour ago, with two precincts still out. County write-in delays, they said. Rural Precinct 9 was always slow; everyone knew that. Except that Precinct 9 was the one that had voted against her in every poll, in every model, in every nightmare. She had come upstairs to fall apart in private, if it came to that. She'd earned the right to lose alone.

The television murmured on the dresser. She'd turned the volume down to almost nothing because the anchors' voices had started to feel like weather report readings of her worth as a human being.

Then the picture changed. Red and blue bars sliding. Her name—WHITFIELD—in large letters.

"—that's it, the county clerk has confirmed. Nine hundred and twelve votes from Precinct Nine in the final tally, and with sixty-one percent of them breaking her way, Nora Whitfield will be the next mayor of Cedarville. Frank, she didn't just win. She *won*."

Nora didn't hear the sound she made. She only knew that her knees had folded and she was on the edge of the bed, phone clutched to her chest like something that might be taken from her.

Eleven months. Eleven months of diners and parking lots and gymnasiums, of shaking hands until her wedding ring left a temporary groove in her finger. Eleven months since the funeral, since she'd stood at the graveside of a man who had run the town's housing office for thirty years and whispered to his casket, *I'm going to finish what you started,* and meant the affordable housing bill he'd died believing in. Robert should have been the candidate. Robert had been too good for the job, everyone said, too honest, and then he was gone, and she had picked up the unfinished thing the way you pick up a coat someone left behind.

Dee was going to scream. Dee had screamed when Nora got the bank loan for her shop, screamed when the divorce was final a decade ago, screamed the good kind of screaming her whole life, and Nora wished—one wild second of wishing—that Robert could hear it too.

She stood. She wiped her face with the heels of her hands. She checked her reflection and laughed at the wreck of it—mascara reapplied in a hotel bathroom at sunrise could only survive so much. She pulled open the door.

Her phone buzzed.

Just one buzz. Unimportant, she almost thought. She almost walked. But her thumb did the antique, automatic thing, and the message opened, and Nora Whitfield stood in the doorway of Room 412 with the sounds of her own victory party rising up through the floor, and did not move for a very long time.

The photo was of her campaign manager, Winnie Okafor, sitting in Robert's office—the office with the Saginaw Bay postcard pinned to the corkboard, the office Nora had not been able to enter for six months after the funeral. Winnie was laughing. Across from her, leaning over the desk with a finger raised as if mid-argument, sat Marcus Thane, the opponent she had beaten three minutes ago. The timestamp was from February. Three weeks before the county audit had "discovered" the deleted housing records that had ended Marcus's career and made Nora's campaign a moral crusade instead of a long shot.

Under the photo, a message from an unsaved number:

*You should ask my husband's wife why she really ran. Check the funding. Check all of it.*

The phone buzzed again. Another message, just four words:

*I know you didn't know.*

Whitney knew. That was the thought that arrived first, the cold one: Winnie had known in February, Winnie had run the oppo research, Winnie had looked Nora in the eye at every restaurant booth and every fundraiser and said *we're clean, we're honest, that's the whole brand*—

A knock at the door made Nora flinch so hard she nearly dropped the phone.

"Nora?" Winnie's voice, bright and breathless, the voice of a woman who has been crying with joy. "Nora, they've been calling you for ten minutes, the whole room is going crazy, it's *time*, honey—"

Through the floor, faint and rising, Nora could hear the crowd begin to chant her name.

On the screen of her phone, Marcus Thane's face stared back from the photo, and Winnie knocked again.

"Nora? Are you decent?"

The doorknob turned.

# John Lennon's Death

John Lennon was murdered on **December 8, 1980**, in New York City. He was shot by Mark David Chapman outside the Dakota, his apartment building on Manhattan's Upper West Side. Lennon was 40 years old.

He and his wife Yoko Ono were returning to their apartment that evening when the shooting occurred. Earlier that same day, Chapman had asked Lennon to sign a copy of the album *Double Fantasy*, which had been released just weeks before. Lennon died from his wounds at nearby Roosevelt Hospital.

The tragedy shocked the world and prompted large-scale mourning, including a famous gathering in Central Park on December 14, 1980, where tens of thousands of fans held a silent vigil.

As part of that, I'd like to mention a couple of underrated examples of things that live in the ocean. Please brainstorm for me a list of a handful of options I can choose from and explain how each is underrated.

content.thinking: The user wants a list of underrated ocean creatures with explanations. Brainstorm a handful with interesting "we don't know much" angles. Format: list with names and short explanations. Medium length, use headers or bold list items.

content.text:
Here are some candidates for your project, each with a note on why it deserves more attention:

**1. Giant Siphonophores**
These are colonial organisms made up of thousands of cloned individual zooids working together as one—sometimes stretching over 100 feet, making them among the longest animals on Earth. Yet most people have never heard of them. They're underrated because they challenge our basic assumptions about what a "single animal" even is, and new species are still being documented by deep-sea submersible dives.

**2. Lampreys**
Often dismissed as "ugly" bloodsuckers, lampreys are actually evolutionary treasures. They're jawless vertebrates whose lineage split from ours over 500 million years ago, making them crucial to understanding vertebrate evolution. They're underrated because their scientific value is obscured by their gross-out reputation.

**3. Zooplankton (as a group)**
Not a single creature, but collectively, zooplankton include organisms like krill, copepods, and the larvae of countless species. They're underrated because they're the invisible foundation of the entire marine food web—most ocean life ultimately depends on them—yet they're often reduced to "whale food" in public imagination.

**4. The Giant Pacific Octopus's cousins (deep-sea octopuses like *Grimpoteuthis*, the "dumbo octopus")**
Deep-sea octopuses are underrated because we've observed relatively few specimens in their natural habitat. Some species have only ever been seen a handful of times, and we still know little about their lifespans, reproduction, or behavior.

**5. Sea Angels (Sea Butterflies)**
These are pteropods—tiny swimming snails with wing-like appendages. They're underrated because they're both beautiful and worrying: their delicate calcium carbonate shells are among the first casualties of ocean acidification, making them sentinels for a major climate threat, yet almost no one outside marine biology circles knows them.

**6. Lugworms and Other Bioturbators**
Underrated champions of the seafloor. Their constant burrowing and sediment-churning genuinely shapes ocean chemistry and nutrient cycling. They're the kind of organism that is ecologically enormous but completely ignored because it lives in mud.

**7. Whale Falls**
Not strictly one organism, but when a whale dies and sinks, its carcass supports entire specialized ecosystems on the abyssal seafloor—some species found at whale falls exist nowhere else. Underrated because each whale fall is essentially a newly discovered habitat, and we've only studied a tiny number of them.

If your project emphasizes "how much we still don't know," whale falls and deep-sea octopuses are probably your strongest picks, since they directly showcase unexplored habitats and undescribed species. If you want to showcase surprises about familiar-sounding things, siphonophores and sea angels make great hooks.

content.text:
# CORN IS IN EVERYTHING (And You Have Michael Pollan to Thank for Knowing It)

## YouTube Video Script

---

**[COLD OPEN]**

**[Fast cuts: corn fields, chips, soda being poured, cereal boxes, gasoline pumps]**

**HOST (direct to camera, low voice):**
Hey. Look at your hand.

**[Beat]**

Go ahead. Look at it. Do you know what's in your body right now? What you had for breakfast? What you had for DINNER?

What if I told you... it was corn. Almost all of it. All of it, in some way.

**[Dramatic music sting]**

**HOST:**
Stay with me — because today, we're talking about a book that changed the way America eats, a journalist who followed a single food chain all the way back to its source, and the crop that secretly conquered the world.

This... is the story of Michael Pollan, The Omnivore's Dilemma... and the KIFICATION of America. You're gonna want to stick around for this one.

---

**[INTRO SEQUENCE / LOGO STING]**

---

**[SECTION 1: WHO IS THIS GUY?]**

**HOST:**
So let's set the scene. The year is 2006. Smartphones don't exist yet. "Organic" just means the expensive aisle at the grocery store. Nobody's philosophizing about their lunch.

Enter Michael Pollan. Now — important thing here — Pollan is not a scientist. He's not a farmer. He's not a dietician. He's a journalist. A writer. Which, honestly? Might be exactly why his book hit so hard.

Because in *The Omnivore's Dilemma*, Pollan does something nobody had really done before. He doesn't just ask "is this food healthy?" He asks a WAY bigger question:

**[Text on screen: "Where does your food actually COME FROM?"]**

He picks four meals — fast food, organic, "pastoral," and a meal he hunts and gathers HIMSELF — and traces every single one back to its origins.

But it's Meal Number One — the fast food meal — where things get absolutely WILD.

---

**[SECTION 2: FOLLOW THE CORN]**

**HOST:**
Pollan buys his family McDonald's. Then he does something kind of unhinged, in the best way.

He sends samples of that fast food... to a LAB. To have it chemically analyzed.

**[Beat. Hold eye contact with camera.]**

And here's where it gets crazy. When the results came back? He found CORN. In everything. The fries contained corn. The soda — obviously corn. The milkshake? Corn. Even the BEEF. The beef had corn in it, because the cattle were RAISED on corn!

**[Quick cuts of corn products stacking up across the screen]**

**HOST:**
And look — maybe you're sitting there like, "Okay, it's corn. Corn is fine. It's a vegetable! It's from the ground! Chill out."

BUT HERE'S THE THING.

It's not just that corn is *in* your food. It's that corn is in EVERYTHING. And Pollan follows the trail to explain HOW.

---

**[SECTION 3: THE SUPER-CROP]**

**HOST:**
You've probably driven past a corn field. You've seen the pictures — tall green stalks, amber waves of grain, very wholesome, very America.

But Pollan introduces you to a version of corn most people have NEVER seen: a scientific Frankenstein of a plant that modern agriculture has made nearly unstoppable.

And this is where you learn about the mind-bending fact of American farming — a fact that sounds like a joke but is devastatingly real:

**[Text on screen: "Corn grows so efficiently that there's TOO MUCH of it."]**

That's right. We grow SO much corn that we have to invent ways to get rid of it. Farmers aren't poor because crops fail — some of them are caught in a system where growing MORE corn keeps prices DOWN — but the system pushes them to keep planting anyway!

So what do we do with a mountain of surplus corn?

**[Music intensifies]**

We feed it to cattle — animals that aren't even BUILT to eat it. We process it into high-fructose corn syrup and pump it into everything from bread to salad dressing. We turn it into additives with names you can't pronounce. Some of it even ends up in things you'd never expect.

Pollan's big insight — the one that'll change how you read a food label — is basically this: walk through a supermarket, and you're not looking at aisles of food. You're looking at a small handful of crops wearing different disguises.

And king among them? Cereal number... let's just say, a LOT of the store is corn in a costume.

---

**[SECTION 4: "GOVERNMENT CORN" — THE PLOT THICKENS]**

**HOST:**
Now, if you're wondering WHY we grow so much of it — great question. Pollan goes there too. He traces it back decades: subsidies, policy, the industrialization of farming after World War Two — a whole machine set in motion that no individual farmer ever really designed, but every farmer has to play along with.

And here's the uncomfortable part. That fast food cheeseburger that's somehow cheaper than a head of broccoli? Pollan argues that price is an illusion. The real costs are just being paid somewhere else — by the environment, by the animals, by your tax dollars... and by YOU, eventually, with your health.

**[Beat]**

I'm not gonna lie to you — this is the part of the video where, if you're eating something right now, you might slowly turn the package over and look at the ingredient list.

That's okay. That's what this book does to you. It's like a food conspiracy thriller, except... it's real, and it's in your pantry.

---

**[SECTION 5: WHY IT MATTERED — THE AFTERMATH]**

**HOST:**
So what happened after The Omnivore's Dilemma dropped?

It didn't just sell books. It helped create a MOVEMENT. Suddenly everyone was talking about farm-to-table. "Local" became a status symbol. People started caring about CAFOs — that's Concentrated Animal Feeding Operations, and no, that's not a pleasant Google search. Documentaries came out. School lunch programs got scrutinized. Farmers' markets boomed.

And Pollan? He distilled his philosophy into one of the most famous food quotes of the 21st century:

**[Text on screen, slowly:] "Eat food. Not too much. Mostly plants."**

Seven words. That's it. That's the whole thing. And yet, incredibly hard to follow when the modern food system seems engineered to do the opposite.

---

**[OUTRO]**

**HOST:**
So — next time you're in the grocery store, do yourself a favor. Flip over a few packages. Read the ingredients. Play the game: how many of these products are secretly corn wearing a hat?

I promise you, once you see it... you CANNOT unsee it. Michael Pollan ruined the supermarket for millions of readers, and honestly? We think you'll thank him for it.

If you want more deep dives into the books that rewired how we think about food, health, and the systems that shape our lives — hit that subscribe button, drop a comment telling me the most SURPRISING ingredient you've ever spotted on a label, and I'll see you in the next one.

**[Beat. Smirk.]**

And hey — it's corn. It was always going to be corn.

**[END SCREEN / OUTRO MUSIC]**

---

### Notes for production:
- **Runtime target:** 8–12 minutes
- **Stock footage needed:** corn fields, McDonald's meals, supercuts of ingredient labels, farmers' markets, drive-through shots
- **Style:** Jump cuts, text overlays for key stats/quotes, escalating music in Sections 2–3
- **Disclaimer suggestion:** A quick on-screen note that the script summarizes Pollan's arguments and reporting, not independent scientific consensus

content.text:
Search Engine Optimization (SEO) is the practice of improving your website so it ranks higher in search engine results on platforms like Google. When someone searches for a product or service you offer, good SEO helps your business appear near the top of those results, making it far more likely that potential customers will click on your site instead of a competitor's.

SEO increases sales by driving free, targeted traffic to your website. Unlike paid ads, organic traffic doesn't cost you per click, which means a better return on investment over time. For example, a local bakery that optimizes its site for searches like "fresh bread near me" can attract nearby customers who are ready to buy. Similarly, an online shoe store that ranks for "comfortable running shoes" reaches shoppers with clear purchasing intent.

Beyond rankings, SEO also improves the overall user experience. Fast-loading pages, mobile-friendly design, and helpful content keep visitors on your site longer, building trust and encouraging purchases. A plumber publishing blog posts answering common questions, for instance, positions themselves as an expert customers feel confident hiring. In short, SEO connects your business with people actively looking for what you sell, turning searches into sales.

nothing in it, for it was only just finished. So she said, “I will wait!” for she was a patient cat, and the summer was before her. She waited a week, and then she climbed up again to the top of the tree, and peeped into the nest. There lay two lovely blue eggs, smooth and shining.

The spotted cat said, “Eggs may be good, but young birds are better. I will wait.” So she waited; and while she was waiting, she caught mice and rats, and washed herself and slept, and did all that a spotted cat should do to pass the time away.

When another week had passed, she climbed the tree again and peeped into the[58] nest. This time there were five eggs. But the spotted cat said again, “Eggs may be good, but young birds are better. I will wait a little longer!”

So she waited a little longer and then went up again to look. Ah! there were five tiny birds, with big eyes and long necks, and yellow beaks wide open. Then the spotted cat sat down on the branch, and licked her nose and purred, for she was very happy. “It is worth while to be patient!” she said.

But when she looked again at the young birds, to see which one she should take first, she saw that they were very thin,—oh, very, very thin they were! The spotted cat had never seen anything so thin in her life.

“Now,” she said to herself, “if I were to wait only a few days longer, they would grow fat. Thin birds may be good, but fat birds are much better. I will wait!”

So she waited; and she watched the father-bird bringing worms all day long to the nest, and said, “Aha! they must be fattening fast! they will soon be as fat as I wish them to be. Aha! what a good thing it is to be patient.”

At last, one day she thought, “Surely, now they must be fat enough! I will not wait another day. Aha! how good they will be!”

So she climbed up the tree, licking her chops all the way and thinking of the fat young birds. And when she reached the top and looked into the nest, it was empty!!

Then the spotted cat sat down on the branch and spoke thus, “Well, of all the horrid, mean, ungrateful creatures I ever saw, those birds are the horridest, and the meanest, and the most ungrateful! Mi-a-u-ow!!!!”

# A Meal Made with Love

Maya stirred the pot of simmering tomato sauce, breathing in the rich aroma of garlic and basil. She'd been planning this dinner for weeks—a special evening just because. No anniversary, no birthday, only the simple desire to see Jake's face light up when he walked through the door.

The chicken parmesan bubbled in the oven, cheese melted to golden perfection. A small candle flickered on the table beside two glasses of red wine, and soft jazz played from the kitchen speaker. She'd even picked fresh parsley from the window sill garden she'd started just for moments like this.

When she heard his key turn in the lock, Maya's heart fluttered. Jake appeared in the kitchen doorway, still in his work jacket, and froze. His tired expression melted into a wide grin.

"What's all this?" he asked, dropping his bag by the door.

"Just dinner," she said, though her smile betrayed how much thought had gone into it.

He crossed the room and wrapped his arms around her from behind, kissing the top of her head. "You're amazing, you know that?"

She laughed and handed him a wooden spoon. "Taste this and tell me if it needs more salt."

"It's perfect," he said. "Just like you."

They ate slowly that night, talking and laughing as the candles burned low—reminded that sometimes the best dinners aren't about the food at all.

content.text:
# The Need for Speed: How Fast Can a Cheetah *Really* Go?

## Meet the Sprinter of the Savanna

If the animal kingdom ever held an Olympics, the cheetah would be the one all the other animals quietly resent. Sleek, spotted, and built like a race car with legs, the cheetah (*Acinonyx jubatus*) is famous for one thing above all: blistering speed. But there's a twist. For decades, we've been telling each other stories about just how fast these cats can go, and it turns out some of those stories were more myth than measurement. Let's take a look at what we *used* to believe versus what science actually tells us now.

## The Tall Tales of Yesterday

Back in the 1930s and beyond, wild claims about cheetah speed ran rampant. One famous measurement from a 1930s track in South Africa clocked a cheetah at a jaw-dropping 71 miles per hour, and later versions of that figure somehow ballooned to an almost supernatural 120 mph in popular retellings. Books, encyclopedias, and classroom posters repeated the "cheap, 70 mph" line for generations. The problem? Nobody exactly parked a radar gun on the savanna. These numbers were based on rough timing over imprecise distances—a cheetah was timed by hand, with hot rods and stopwatches, chasing lures like a greyhound on a track. The methodology was shaky at best, and the numbers stuck around because, frankly, they sounded awesome.

## What the Science Says Now

Fast-forward to the 2000s and 2010s, when researchers finally gave cheetahs the Formula 1 treatment. The most famous test subject was a cheetah named Sarah at the Cincinnati Zoo, who wore a high-tech collar with an onboard accelerometer. In 2012, Sarah was clocked running a peak speed of 58 to 61 miles per hour—still blazingly fast, just a bit short of the legendary 70. Then a landmark study published in *Nature* in 2013 tracked wild cheetahs in Botswana with GPS collars and found something surprising: most hunting cheetahs don't even hit top speed in the wild! Their average maximum was around 33 miles per hour, with speed actually being *less* important to a successful hunt than being able to accelerate and decelerate sharply.

## The Magic Is in the Launch

So if cheetahs aren't spending all day at 60 mph, what's the real secret? Accuracy over top speed. Wild cheetahs in the study routinely made sharp, agile turns at high speed, pulling lateral forces of up to 13 Gs—more than a fighter pilot experiences! Sarah, ever the overachiever, also showed off a 0 to 60 mph acceleration in about 3 seconds, rivalling the world's fastest production sports cars. So while yesterday's facts oversold the top speed, they undersold the truly bonkers part: how a cheetah *gets* to whatever speed it's going.

## The Verdict: Still the Champ

Even after science shaved a few miles per hour off the record books, the cheetah remains the undisputed fastest land animal on Earth—no other land creature comes close. The contrast between past and present tells us a valuable story, too: sometimes the truth is a little more nuanced than the legend, but still plenty impressive. A cat that can out-accelerate a Ferrari, corner like a race car, and do it all while wearing a permanent grin? The legend earns its stripes—er, spots—either way.

**The Great Train Robbery (1903)** is one of the most important films in cinema history—a short silent Western directed by Edwin S. Porter, running about 12 minutes. It's widely considered a landmark because it helped establish narrative filmmaking as we know it.

**The plot:** The film tells a simple story of outlaws who hold up a train in the American West. The bandits force the telegraph operator to stop the train, board it, and rob the passengers before escaping on horseback. Meanwhile, a little girl discovers the wounded telegraph operator, who alerts a posse. The posse pursues the bandits in a shootout, and the criminals are ultimately gunned down.

**Why it was significant:**
- It's often cited as one of the first narrative films with a clear, multi-scene storyline rather than a single continuous shot of an event.
- It pioneered techniques like editing between different locations, cross-cutting between simultaneous actions, and location shooting.
- It featured an early experiment in color (hand-tinted frames) and the famous final shot: a bandit firing his pistol directly at the camera, which startled audiences of the era.

It was enormously popular and helped launch the Western genre.

# The Question

Tomas wiped his boots three times on the mat before knocking on Hollis's door — a habit he'd picked up from watching the old man plant, where every motion seemed measured against some invisible standard.

Hollis opened the door before the third knock landed, as if he'd been expecting him since dawn.

"You're growing tomatoes again," Hollis said. Not a question.

"Third year. Third failure." Tomas held out a tomato as evidence — small, split-skinned, pale as a lie. "I've read every book. I test my soil. I water on schedule."

Hollis took the tomato and turned it over in his weathered hands like a jeweler assessing a flawed stone. Then he said nothing for so long that Tomas began to wonder if he'd been forgotten.

"Do you eat them?" Hollis finally asked.

"What? The tomatoes? You can't eat these things."

"That's your problem." Hollis handed the tomato back. "You grow them like they're appointments on a calendar. Grow them like you're going to eat them, like you're hungry for them, and you'll taste when they're thirsty. You'll notice the leaves going yellow before the books say you should. The garden doesn't read your schedule, boy. It reads your attention."

Tomas opened his mouth to protest — he *did* pay attention, he'd spent whole afternoons crouched between rows — but Hollis was already shuffling toward the kitchen, waving him along.

"Sit. You'll stay for dinner. I'm making sauce." He paused at the stove and looked back with the ghost of a smile. "My tomatoes. Grown for eating, not for growing. You'll see the difference on your tongue before I explain a single thing."

The sauce, Tomas had to admit, changed everything. No book had ever tasted like that.

He walked home in the dark, and for the first time in three years, he couldn't wait to get his hands in the dirt — not to follow the plan, but to *pay attention*.

content.text:
On August 24, 1814, during the War of 1812, British forces captured Washington, D.C., and burned several U.S. government buildings. This included the White House, the U.S. Capitol, and other public buildings such as the Treasury. The burning was in retaliation for the American destruction of buildings in York (now Toronto), Upper Canada.

Key details:

- **The White House** (then called the President's House) was set on fire, along with its interior contents. Dolley Madison is famously credited with saving the portrait of George Washington (a copy of the Lansdowne portrait by Gilbert Stuart) before fleeing.
- **The Capitol building**, housing the Library of Congress and the Supreme Court, was burned, destroying the original Library of Congress collection.
- President **James Madison** and other government officials had fled the city shortly before the British arrived.

A sudden, violent thunderstorm the following day helped extinguish some of the fires. The destruction prompted discussions about moving the capital, but ultimately Washington was rebuilt on the same site, and theevent spurred the completion of the Capitol and White House restorations in the years that followed.

- **English Mastiff**: Generally considered the heaviest breed, with adult males typically weighing 150–230 pounds (some individuals have exceeded 340 pounds)
- **Great Dane**: Usually the tallest breed. The record-holder, a Dane named Zeus, stood 44 inches (111.8 cm) at the shoulder
- **Irish Wolfhound** and **Tibetan Mastiff** are also among the biggest breeds

## Lifespan: Large vs. Small Dogs

Yes, there is a significant difference — and it's somewhat counterintuitive:

**Large dogs live shorter lives, on average.**

| Dog Size | Typical Lifespan |
|----------|-----------------|
| Small breeds (Chihuahua, Toy Poodle) | 12–16+ years |
| Medium breeds (Beagle, Bulldog) | 10–14 years |
| Giant breeds (Great Dane, Mastiff) | 7–10 years |

**Why does this happen?**

1. **Faster aging**: Large dogs seem to age at an accelerated rate — their bodies essentially "burn through" their lifespans more quickly
2. **Rapid growth**: Giant breeds grow extremely fast as puppies, which may put stress on developing joints and organs
3. **Size-related health issues**: Larger dogs are more prone to conditions like:
   - Bone and joint problems (hip dysplasia, arthritis)
   - Bloat (gastric torsion), which is life-threatening
   - Heart conditions (e.g., dilated cardiomyopathy)
   - Certain cancers

Some research suggests that for every additional ~4.4 pounds (2 kg) of body weight, a dog's lifespan decreases by roughly one month.

One interesting exception: mixed-breed dogs of various sizes often live slightly longer than purebreds of comparable size, likely due to greater genetic diversity.

messages.content: Can you give me some of the most common causes of kidney or renal failure?

content.text:
# Common Causes of Kidney (Renal) Failure

Kidney failure generally develops in two ways: **acute** (sudden) and **chronic** (gradual). Here are the main causes of each:

## Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) — Leading Causes

1. **Diabetes** – The most common cause, accounting for roughly 40–50% of cases. High blood sugar damages the kidney's filtering units over time.
2. **High blood pressure (hypertension)** – The second leading cause. Constant high pressure damages blood vessels in the kidneys.
3. **Glomerulonephritis** – Inflammation of the kidney's filtering structures (glomeruli).
4. **Polycystic kidney disease** – An inherited condition causing fluid-filled cysts that impair kidney function.
5. **Prolonged urinary obstruction** – From kidney stones, enlarged prostate, or tumors.
6. **Recurrent kidney infections** (pyelonephritis)

## Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) — Common Triggers

1. **Reduced blood flow to the kidneys** – Severe dehydration, blood loss, heart failure, or septic shock.
2. **Direct kidney damage** – Certain medications (e.g., NSAIDs, some antibiotics, contrast dyes), toxins, or severe infections.
3. **Urinary blockage** – Kidney stones, blood clots, or bladder obstruction.

## Other Contributing Factors

- **Autoimmune diseases** – Lupus (lupus nephritis) is a notable example.
- **Smoking, obesity, and high cholesterol** – These increase risk and worsen underlying conditions.
- **Family history** of kidney disease
- **Age** – Risk increases significantly after 60.

## Key Takeaway

Diabetes and hypertension together cause the majority of chronic kidney failure cases — which is why managing blood sugar and blood pressure is so important for prevention. Early kidney disease often has no symptoms, so regular screening matters if you have risk factors.

Would you like more detail on any of these, or information on symptoms or prevention?

content.text:
# The Quiet Ones

I have always been good at noticing things other people miss. The way a stranger's smile doesn't reach her eyes. The way a man checks the street before entering his own home—as if he's forgotten which direction safety comes from. These small tells are everywhere, once you learn to look. Most people never learn to look. That's what makes them easy.

I work at a print shop downtown. Nobody remembers my name, though they see me every day. There's a particular kind of invisibility that comes from being unremarkable, and I cultivated it the way a gardener cultivates moss—in darkness, patiently, where it flourishes best. I wear gray. I say "have a good one" instead of goodbye. I let doors close in my face rather than hold them, because people remember small kindnesses, and kindness leaves a trace.

Marge at the coffee shop remembers my order but not my face. That took two years to achieve.

I want to tell you about the pond behind my mother's old house, though I suppose that's backwards. I should tell you about the pond first, and then you'd understand everything else. When I was nine, I found a bird there— dokonale intact, floating, its wings folded neatly as if it were sleeping. I waded in to retrieve it. I remember the cold climbing my legs, the way the mud held my ankles like fingers. I brought the bird home and kept it in a shoebox under my bed for eleven days. I told no one. It was the first thing that was entirely mine.

My mother found it, eventually. She screamed. She called me a little monster while I stood very still, and I remember thinking, with peculiar clarity, that the word didn't fit. Monsters are loud. Monsters wreck rooms. I had kept the bird clean. I had kept it safe. If anything, the monster was whoever had let it drown.

The police held a press conference last month. I watched it on the bar television, a strangers' faces soft with importance. Detective Reyes—I've learned her name now, which is a failure on my part, or hers—said the words *we believe the same individual is responsible*. The bar murmured. Someone near me crossed herself. I ordered another drink and thought about how strange it is, that sound the city makes when it begins to be afraid. A held breath. A thousand windows checking their locks at the same hour.

I don't think of them as victims. That word belongs to Detective Reyes, to the anchors, to the mothers who give tearful interviews with their collars clutched in one fist. To me, they are the quiet ones—people who moved through the world leaving wakes but never looking back at the ripples. People who had stopped noticing things. The world is full of them. It always has been.

There is a woman at the library on Fourth Street. She goes on Tuesdays. She reads the way some people pray, with her whole face opened. She returns her books on time—I checked, once, the receipt still tucked in the cover—and she always sits by the window where the light is best, and she never once looks to see who is sitting behind her.

I have not decided about her yet. I want to be honest about that, because I suspect you assume the decision is made the moment I notice someone, and it isn't. Noticing is only the beginning. Noticing is as far as the bird went, for years. The rest—the box, the keeping—that arrived later, the way winter arrives, undeniable and on no schedule you get to set.

Some nights I walk home the long way, past the harbor, and I watch the water move. People think the sea is peaceful. It isn't. It's indifferent, which is a different and grander thing. It takes what it takes and never once explains itself, and still they build their little houses facing it, still they bring their children to stand at its edge.

Detective Reyes said in her press conference that this individual wants attention. She said it with confidence, and the cameras loved it, and she was wrong in the way that matters most. I don't want attention. Attention is a net. What I want is for someone, someday, to look at the quiet ones the way I looked at that bird—to understand that they were kept, that they were mine, that someone in this whole indifferent world held them carefully at the end.

The woman at the library reads by the window on Tuesdays.

Tomorrow is Tuesday.

## 1. Dark Chocolate or Unsweetened Cocoa
A small square of dark chocolate (or a tablespoon of cocoa powder) melts into the chili and adds a deep, rich, slightly smoky undertone. A shot of espresso or a half cup of brewed coffee amplifies the savory, meaty depth of the chili. It pairs beautifully with the chile powder and creates a richer, almost barbecue-like flavor. Okay, let me give you a real third option: **a splash of whiskey or bourbon**, deglazed into the pot. content.text:
# The Last Night at Maxwell's
*As told by Steve Fallon, owner*

When I started booking bands in my little bar down in Hoboken thirty-five years ago, the town was known for exactly one thing: being the birthplace of Frank Sinatra. Nobody came here for music. Nobody came here for much of anything, really. But I had this tiny, plain bar — nothing fancy, just a room — and I figured, why not give it a shot?

I couldn't have imagined what would happen next.

People sometimes say the strangest things about the place. Chris Stamey, an old Hoboken resident and one of the many musicians who've mourned our passing, told me Maxwell's felt like "a Portkey in Harry Potter." I had to laugh at that — but I suppose I understand what he meant. You'd grab hold of the place, and it would whisk you somewhere else entirely. Somewhere bigger. Somewhere magical.

Because that's what Maxwell's became. When people talk about the great rock clubs — Max's Kansas City, CBGB, the Bottom Line — they talk about New York City. But I'll tell you something: Maxwell's ranks as high as any of them, even though our legal address was always New Jersey.

Over the years, we saw it all. Countless nights of weird, wonderful music from acts nobody had heard of — until suddenly, everybody had heard of them. Nirvana played here. R.E.M. played here. And then there were the nights that didn't go anywhere at all. The New Marines once drew exactly one paying customer. One. I remember it. Those nights are part of the story too.

On July 31st, it all comes full circle. The Bongos — along with a — were the first bands ever to perform at Maxwell's, and they'll be the last. A final show. Then the doors close.

Thirty-five years. A bar that was supposed to be just a bar. I wouldn't trade a single night of it.

messages.content: Create a story about a family of cardinals defending their nest from a hungry cat.

content.text:
# The Red Watchers

The morning sun filtered through the oak leaves as Cardinal Marlowe perched on the highest branch, his crimson feathers blazing against the green canopy. Below him, his mate Celeste nestled in their carefully woven home, three speckled eggs glowing warm beneath her soft wing.

Marlowe had learned long ago to read the subtle warnings of the forest. The chattering of squirrels. The sudden silence of songbirds. So when the finches stopped singing all at once, his head snapped toward the sounds below.

Charts. A rusty-brown tabby with pale green eyes.

The cat moved with terrible patience, slinking through the ferns at the base of the oak tree. Her oversized paws made no sound on the fallen leaves.

"Celeste," Marlowe chirped low, a note of danger in his voice. "Stay with the eggs. Do not move."

The cat began to climb.

Marlowe launched himself from his perch like a crimson arrow. He raked past the tabby's whiskers with a furious cry, his talons grazing her nose. The cat flinched but kept climbing, her claws finding purchase in the bark.

Then cam the sound that made even the brave Marlowe's heart jump—the frantic alarm of the neighborhood birds. The chickadees arrived first, dive-bombing in a rapid squadron. A mockingbird joined in, shrieking like a hawk to frighten the predator. Even the tiny hummingbird hovering menacingly near the cat's ear seemed to hiss.

But the tabby was stubborn, and she was closer now. Marlowe's eyes burned with determination. He could see his reflection in those pale green eyes—his family, his home, everything precious to him balanced in those three eggs.

With a battle cry that startled even himself, Marlowe struck again and again, a flustered whirlwind of red. Celeste left the nest now, her amber wings joining the assault. Together they pecked at the cat's ears and tail while the mockingbird swooped between her paws.

The tabby, overwhelmed by the buzzing storm of feathers, lost her grip. She tumbled backward through the ferns, scrambled up, and fled across the meadow with her tail low, humiliated by creatures a tenth her size.

The mighty oak fell silent once more. Slowly, the small army of defenders dispersed, returning to their own lives.

Marlowe sank onto the branch beside his nest, wings heavy but his heart full. Celeste preened his ruffled feathers gently, the way she always did after they'd fought off the world together.

Below them, hidden in the ferns, the tabby licked a scratch on her nose and promised herself she'd find easier prey tomorrow.

But for today, the eggs slept safe and warm, guarded by their crimson sentinels.

content.thinking: Simple question about paint types and cleanability. Answer: semi-gloss/gloss paints, especially latex/semi-gloss. Explain briefly.

content.text:
For easy cleaning, **semi-gloss and gloss paints** are your best options. Here's a quick breakdown:

**Most washable options:**
- **High-gloss paint** – The most durable and easiest to wipe clean, thanks to its hard, non-porous surface. Great for trim, doors, and high-traffic areas, but it shows imperfections and reflects a lot of light.
- **Semi-gloss paint** – A popular choice for kitchens, bathrooms, and kids' rooms. It's very scrubbable while being slightly less shiny than high-gloss.
- **Satin (eggshell-satin) paint** – A good middle ground. It offers decent cleanability with a softer, more subtle sheen, making it popular for hallways and living areas.

**Hardest to clean:**
- **Flat and matte paints** – While great at hiding wall imperfections, their porous, chalky finish absorbs stains and can burnish (shiny spots) when scrubbed, so they're the most difficult to wipe down.

**A few extra tips:**
- **Latex (water-based) paints** labeled as "scrubbable" or "washable" are generally easier to maintain than oil-based options when it comes to cleaning up both the wall and your tools.
- Look for paints marketed as **"stain-resistant"** or **"easy-clean"** — many modern brands (especially premium lines) use advanced acrylic formulas that resist stains even in flatter finishes.
- kitchens, bathrooms, and children's rooms benefit most from glossier finishes, while bedrooms and ceilings often do fine with flat or matte.

If cleanability is your top priority, semi-gloss on the walls or high-gloss on trim is the way to go.

content.text:
West-side San Francisco (the Sunset and Richmond districts) has a unique microclimate: heavy fog, cool temperatures, and often indirect or filtered light. The good news is that many plants actually thrive in these conditions. Here's a list of options:

1. **Kale** – One of the best edibles for low light. It tolerates fog well and actually prefers cool weather, often tasting sweeter after foggy, damp conditions.

2. **Lettuce and other salad greens** – Lettuce, arugula, and mustard greens all bolt less in cool, dim conditions, meaning you get a longer harvest window than gardeners in sunny climates.

3. **Swiss chard** – Very forgiving of low light and produces continuously for months. The rainbow varieties add color to a shady yard.

4. **Spinach** – Thrives in cool, foggy conditions and will struggle only if it gets too much heat and sun, which isn't a problem on the west side.

5. **Mint** – Practically thrives on neglect and shade. Just plant it in a container, as it spreads aggressively in the ground. Great for tea and cocktails.

6. **Parsley and cilantro** – Both herbs handle partial shade well. Cilantro actually bolts *less* in cool fog, so you'll get more leafy harvest before it flowers.

7. **Chives** – One of the most shade-tolerant alliums and comes back year after year.

8. **Rhubarb** – A classic shade-tolerant perennial. It loves the cool, moist climate and comes back bigger every year.

9. **Evergreen huckleberry** – A California native shrub that produces edible berries and genuinely prefers partial to full shade. Well-suited to fog belt gardens.

10. **Salmonberry or thimbleberry** – Native shade-tolerant brambles that produce soft, raspberry-like fruit and handle coastal fog natively.

11. **Nasturtiums** – Edible flowers and leaves with a peppery bite. They tolerate shade, bloom generously, and self-seed readily.

content.text:
# The Brady Bunch — Answers

**1. The premise**
The show (which aired on ABC from 1969–1974) was about the creation and daily life of a modern blended family. Architect Mike Brady, a widowed father of three boys (Greg, Peter, and Bobby), married Carol, a mother of three girls (Marcia, Jan, and Cindy). Together with the boys' dog, Tiger, and their live-in housekeeper Alice Nelson, the newly blended family of eight navigated everyday problems in their suburban home — the whole family famously sharing one bathroom.

**2. The previous spouses**
This was famously left vague on the show. It was strongly implied that Mike's first wife had died, though it was never explicitly discussed. Carol's first husband was never mentioned at all — no explanation of death, divorce, or anything else. Series creator Sherwood Schwartz later said he had always intended Carol to be a divorcée, but network concerns made the show avoid acknowledging divorce entirely (a controversial subject for primetime family TV at the time).

**3. How long it ran**
Five seasons, from September 1969 to March 1974, producing 117 episodes. Ironically, its modest ratings during its original run led to its cancellation — yet the show became enormously popular in syndicated reruns, arguably becoming more famous afterward than during its broadcast life. It spawned multiples sequels, reunion specials, movies, and spin-offs.

**4. Whatever happened to Tiger?**
Sadly, the dog was written out after the first season. According to series creator Sherwood Schwartz, the dog that played Tiger was hit by a car and died while producing early episodes of season two. Compounding the bad luck, the doghouse set off the patio was destroyed in an accident around the same time. Rather than recast the dog and rebuild the set, the show simply wrote Tiger out — and he was never mentioned again.

Once upon a time, the Sun and the Moon were best friends. But they had never talked about their feelings.

"Moon, I love your soft, silvery light," said the Sun.

"And I love your warm, golden glow," said the Moon.

From that day on, they made a promise: whenever something worried them, they would talk about it right away.

And now, every day, as the Sun sets, he whispers "Goodnight, friend!" to the Moon. And the Moon smiles down at everyone as she says, "Good morning, friend!"

**The End.**

*Message for little readers: Talking honestly with friends solves problems and keeps friendships glowing!*

Based on the source text, here's how the CDC's changes to COVID-19 data collection will affect reliability:

## What's Being Lost

**Percent positivity and community levels tracking:** The CDC will stop tracking the percentage of tests that come back positive, which was used to calculate transmission rates. Without this data, real-time transmission tracking will likely become less precise, since percent positivity is a near-real-time indicator of how widely the virus is spreading.

**Detailed hospital data:** Hospitals will no longer be required to report the number of cases, or the race, sex, and age of patients. Losing demographic breakdowns makes it harder to detect disparities in how COVID-19 affects different populations, and losing hospital-level case counts reduces the granularity of the data.

**Legal authority for data collection:** Much of this stems from the end of the public health emergency on May 11. That designation gave the CDC the power to *demand* certain data from states—without it, the CDC can't compel states to report at the same level, so data may be less complete or less voluntarily submitted.

## What Remains Reliable

**Death data will still be highly accurate**, just slower. The CDC will now rely on the National Vital Statistics System, which officials describe as highly accurate, but it lags other surveillance by two to three weeks. So death figures remain trustworthy, but you won't know about surges as quickly.

**Hospitalizations and ICU admissions** will still be tracked in aggregate, which preserves an important, consistent measure of severe disease—though without case counts and demographics attached.

## The Bottom Line

The CDC's argument, summarized by Dr. Nirav Shah's snowflake metaphor, is that reliability will shift in *nature* rather than disappear: the picture will still show overall trends ("it's snowing") but with less detail and timeliness (not "counting every snowflake"). In practical terms, expect data that is still directionally reliable for tracking major trends in severe disease, but less detailed, slower to reflect changes, and less able to show who exactly is being affected or how quickly transmission is growing.

messages.content: Once released from the Committee stage, what happens to a bill before it is sent over to the Senate to begin its journey again?

content.thinking: The question asks about US legislative process—Committee stage, then floor action in the House beforeSenate.

content.text:
After a bill passes through the House committee stage, it must still clear several steps before moving to the Senate:

## Floor Action in the House

1. **Rules Committee consideration** – Because the House has strict procedures, most bills must first go to the House Rules Committee, which sets the conditions for debate. The Rules Committee decides:
   - How much time will be allotted for debate
   - Whether amendments may be offered (open rule vs. closed rule)
   - When the bill will come to the floor

2. **House floor debate and vote** – The bill is then debated by the full House under those rules, and members vote. If a simple majority approves it, the bill passes the House.

## Transmission to the Senate

Once passed, the bill is officially sent ("engrossed" and messaged) to the Senate, typically carried over by the Clerk officially announced to the Senate chamber.

## Important note: "Beginning its journey again"

There's a nuance here—when the bill arrives in the Senate, it doesn't always start completely over. The Senate sometimes:

- **Considers the House bill directly** through its own committee and floor process, *or*
- **Takes up the House bill but substitutes its own version** as an amendment (a common procedural shortcut), or
- **Uses the "ping-pong" method**, where the House simply votes on the Senate's final version to save time

If the Senate passes the same bill text unchanged, it goes directly to the President. If the Senate amends it, the bill must return to the House for **conference committee** negotiations to reconcile the two versions before final passage by both chambers.

content.text:
**The Tenant**

It arrived quietly, the way mold arrives in the walls of a drowning house. Marta did not see it settle in. She only noticed, one gray February morning, that her hands had grown heavy—that lifting them required a labor she could not name.

The parasite fed on warmth first. It found the heat of her laughter—dormant for months—and drained the last of it through her chest, slowly, the way a tick drinks. Where it attached itself, the tissue of her days turned gray and dried. Breakfast became a thing done to someone else. Her daughter's voice reached her as if heard through silt and water, muffled, distant, already fading.

It grew. Of course it grew. Parasites do.

It threaded itself along her spine like ivy along a fence, rootlets gripping nerve and memory alike. It learned her rhythms and settled into them, heavier at dusk, heavier after phone calls, heavier whenever anyone asked, *Are you all right?*—a question it answered for her with a smile calibrated to end the conversation. It wore her face in public. She was only the skin stretched over it.

She could feel it eating now, a cold gnawing beneath the ribs, meticulous, patient. It consumed the color of her kitchen, then the meaning of her books, then the memory of why she had ever stood by this window at all. Some hosts burn out. Some hosts starve the thing by starving themselves. Marta did neither. She simply sat, and let it feed, because the struggle had been consumed too—one of the first meals it took from her, and she had not even noticed that course.

At night, it grew bold. She could hear it in her own voice when she said *I'm fine*—a wet, contented gurgling, deep in the throat. It was happy, insofar as such a thing can be. It wanted nothing more than what it had: a host, still breathing, still warm enough to keep it alive through another gray winter.

In the spring, someone found her sitting by the window, limbs thin as paper, hollowed clean.

The tenant, well-fed and glistening, slid out through the cracks of her and went looking for the next warm room.

It always found one.

# Family Game Night Shopping List

Great idea for a family tradition! Here's a mix of classics and newer hits that work well for kids 8+ and adults alike.

## Classic Favorites
1. **Monopoly** – The quintessential property-trading game (consider Monopoly Junior if attention spans are shorter)
2. **Scrabble** – Great for building vocabulary and spelling skills
3. **Clue** – A fun whodunit mystery where players deduce the culprit
4. **Sorry!** – Simple, fast-paced racing game with just enough luck
5. **Battleship** – Head-to-head deduction game of guessing ship locations
6. **Risk** – World domination strategy game (games can run long)
7. **Connect Four** – Quick and easy, great as a warm-up game
8. **Yahtzee** – Dice-rolling classic that's easy to learn
9. **Chess or Checkers** – Timeless two-player strategy

## Modern Hits
10. **Ticket to Ride** – Collect train cards to claim railway routes across a map; one of the best gateway games
11. **Catan** – Trade resources and build settlements; a modern classic
12. **Carcassonne** – Lay tiles to build a medieval landscape with cities and roads
13. **Splendor** – Collect gems to purchase development cards; quick to learn
14. **Azul** – Beautiful tile-drafting game with simple rules
15. **Kingdomino** – Build your kingdom with domino-style tiles; quick and fun
16. **Sushi Go!** – Fast, fun card-drafting game that plays in 15 minutes

## Cooperative Games (Everyone Plays Together)
17. **Forbidden Island** – Work as a team to grab treasures before the island sinks
18. **Pandemic** – Team up to stop global disease outbreaks; very satisfying to win together

19. **Telestrations** – Broken telephone meets sketching; hilarious with families

content.text:
# What Are Stocks?

Stocks (also called shares or equities) are units of ownership in a company. When you buy a stock, you purchasing a small piece of that business—you become a **shareholder** or **part-owner**.

## How They Work

When companies need money to grow, they can sell portions of ownership to the public through **stock exchanges** like the NYSE or NASDAQ. Investors buy these shares hoping the company will succeed.

## How You Can Make Money

1. **Capital gains** – If the company's value grows, your stock becomes worth more. Buy at $50, sell at $75, and you profit $25 per share.
2. **Dividends** – Some companies share profits with shareholders through regular payments, often quarterly.

## Key Things to Know

- **Risk**: Stock prices fluctuate daily. You can lose money if prices fall.
- **Ownership perks**: Shareholders may vote on company decisions and receive annual reports.
- **Diversification**: Investors typically spread money across many stocks to reduce risk.
- **Long-term vs. short-term**: Prices are volatile in the short term but have historically grown over decades.

## An Example

Imagine Pizza Co. issues 1,000,000 shares. If you buy 100 shares, you own 0.01% of the company. If it opens 50 new locations and profits soar, demand for its stock may rise—increasing your shares' value.

Would you like to know more about how to invest, types of stocks, or how stock markets work?

The golden meadows of home were gone, replaced by a grim and shadowy land I did not recognize, full of pale-faced strangers who stared at me with cold, unsmiling eyes. I clutched my mother's crystal pendant to my chest and whispered a wish into the wind, but no magic answered me. My wings, once bright as dawn, quivered with fear against my back.

Above me, the sky rumbled and cracked, for thunderstorms rolled endlessly across this dark place, drenching everything in cold grey rain. Strange beastly creatures lurked between the twisted trees—things with glowing amber eyes and claws that scraped against stone—sniffing the air as if searching for something, or someone. I pressed myself against the hollow of an ancient oak, my heart hammering like the thunder itself, and I wondered desperately how I had come to be here and whether I would ever find my way back to Aldenland. But deep inside me, beneath all the trembling, a small voice reminded me that a fairy princess of Aldenland does not give up—not even here. content.text:
# Sci-Fi Weapon Ideas: Non-Bullet Projectiles

Here's a list of realistic alternatives, roughly ordered from most to least "hard sci-fi" plausible:

## 1. Ferrous Slug Accelerator (Coilgun/Railgun)
Technically still a projectile, but it's not a bullet — it's a iron磁 or tungsten rod launched via electromagnets. No gunpowder, no casing, no recoil from gas expansion. Instead, it uses a sequence of energized coils that "pull" the slug down the barrel.
- **Downside to address:** Heat buildup in the coils and massive power draw. A removed heat-sink magazine is a great flavor detail.

## 2. Particle Beam Weapon
Accelerates subatomic particles (electrons, protons, or ions) to near light speed using electromagnetic fields. On impact, the beam deposits thermal radiation, essentially cooking the target from the inside.
- **Realism note:** These actually exist in lab settings; the challenge is atmospherics. Atmospheric particle beams bloom and lose focus, which you can either hand-wave with future tech or use as a built-in limitation (e.g., poor in fog or rain).

## 3. Plasma Bolt Launcher
Fires a small packet of superheated ionized gas, contained magnetically for a fraction of a second before it disperses. Think of it as throwing a tiny, short-lived star.
- **Realism note:** Physicists point out plasma dissipates almost instantly in atmosphere, so your gun would need to imply a magnetic containment field that only lasts long enough to cross a room. That limitation actually makes the weapon feel more credible.

## 4. Directed Sonic Weapon
Uses a focused acoustic beam to rupture eardrums, cause disorientation, or (at higher power) damage internal organs. This is real tech today — LRAD systems used by police work exactly this way.
- **Strengths:** Silent to anyone outside the cone, nonlethal settings available.
- **Weaknesses:** Slow to act, ineffective against targets wearing ear protection, and air absorbs high frequencies quickly.

## 5. Maser (Microwave Laser)
Projects a concentrated beam of microwave radiation that heats water molecules in the target's body, causing excruciating burns and potentially cardiac disruption. The U.S. military has already deployed an anti-personnel microwave system called the Active Denial System.
- **Great for:** A "clean" energy weapon that leaves no visible wounds — only internal damage. Corners for mystery or forensics tropes.

## 6. Super-Heated Liquid Metal Injector
Fires droplets of molten metal (or a chemical that ignites on contact with air) via electromagnetic induction, essentially a gun-sized flamethrower with no flame trail until impact.
- **Flavor advantage:** Unique visual signature — glowing perforations rather than bullet holes.

## 7. Coherent Light Lance (High-End Laser)
Unlike movie lasers, a *real* high-powered laser weapon wouldn't be visible in flight and would work by burning a hole in milliseconds of contact. The pulse duration matters more than "beam" imagery.
- **Realism note:** Pulsed lasers that ablate material in nanoseconds are more practical than continuous beams, which can be blocked by cheap mirrors or smoke. Scoping your weapon this way makes it feel researched.

## 8. Cryo-Agent Projector
Compressed liquid nitrogen or a similar cryogenic fluid launched in a hypercooled aerosol stream. Frostbite, brittleness of materials, and equipment failure — kills by thermal shock rather than trauma.
- **Best used as:** A niche anti-drone or anti-vehicle weapon, since extreme cold kills electronics and engines more readily than it kills humans quickly.

## 9. Electro-Pulse Launcher (Nonlethal)
Fires small projectiles that embed in skin or clothing, then discharge a high-voltage capacitive shock — basically a self-contained, long-range Taser round. This technology (the Taser XREP round) existed commercially.
- **Perfect for:** Characters who need to disable rather than kill, like bounty hunters or law enforcement.

## 10. Chemical Dart Streams
Compressed-gas-driven microdarts carrying agents: paralytics, sedatives, coagulants, or combat drugs. The "bullets" are drug payloads, and choosing the payload is choosing the effect.
- **Story advantage:** Great for espionage settings — a hit that looks like a heart attack.

---

**A tip for believability:** Whatever you choose, give it one or two *grounded limitations* — heat management, power supply, effective range, or atmospheric interference. Sci-fi weapons feel most realistic when they behave like machines with tradeoffs, not magic wands.

Want me to expand on any of these — like the physics of railguns, or how a plasma bolt could plausibly work?

# Common Early Pregnancy Symptoms

Here are the most frequently reported symptoms during early pregnancy:

## Physical Symptoms

- **Missed period** – Often the first and most reliable sign
- **Nausea/vomiting** – "Morning sickness," though it can occur any time of day (commonly starts 4–6 weeks after conception)
- **Breast changes** – Tenderness, swelling, darkened nipples/areolas, or a sense of heaviness
- **Fatigue** – Extreme tiredness, largely due to rising progesterone levels
- **Frequent urination** – Increased blood flow and kidney activity
- **Bloating and constipation** – Hormone-related slowing of digestion
- **Spotting or light bleeding** – Implantation bleeding (when the embryo attaches, typically 10–14 days after conception)
- **Cramping** – Mild uterine cramps as the uterus begins to change
- **Food aversions or cravings** – Sudden dislike of foods or smells once tolerated
- **Heightened smell sensitivity** – Some odors may seem stronger or unpleasant
- **Dizziness or lightheadedness** – Often related to blood pressure and blood sugar changes

## Other Signs

- **Mood swings** – Hormonal fluctuations can affect emotions
- **Headaches** – Common due to hormonal shifts
- **Metallic taste in the mouth** – Reported by some people
- **Elevated basal body temperature** – Staying high past the expected period date

## Important Notes

- Symptoms vary widely from person to person and pregnancy to pregnancy
- Some people experience very few or no early symptoms
- Many of these symptoms overlap with premenstrual symptoms

**A home pregnancy test after a missed period followed by a visit to a healthcare provider is the best way to confirm pregnancy.** If you suspect you may be pregnant, consult a medical professional for guidance.

content.text:
## What Is Cryptozoology?

Cryptozoology is the study of "hidden animals" — creatures that some people claim exist, but that science has never proven are real. The word comes from Greek: *kryptos* (hidden), *zos* (animal), and *logos* (study). Cryptozoologists search for legendary beasts like Bigfoot and the Loch Ness Monster using footprints, blurry photos, eyewitness stories, and strange sounds in the night. Scientists are usually skeptical — but Hey, people once thought gorillas and giant squid were just myths, too!

---

## Four Legendary Creatures

### 🦶 1. Bigfoot (Sasquatch)
**The Legend:** Deep in the forests of the Pacific Northwest lives a massive, ape-like creature standing 7 to 10 feet tall, covered in dark shaggy hair. Hikers report finding footprints 16 inches long — much bigger than any human shoe. Sometimes campers hear loud, eerie howls echoing between the trees at night... and swear something huge is watching them from the shadows, just out of reach of their flashlight beam.

**The Creepy Part:** Bigfoot has supposedly been spotted thousands of times, yet no body, bones, or clear photo has *ever* been found. It's as if something out there knows exactly how to stay hidden.

---

### 🐊 2. The Chupacabra
**The Legend:** This creature's name means "goat sucker" in Spanish. First reported in Puerto Rico in 1995, it's described as a reptile-like beast with spines down its back and glowing red eyes — or sometimes like a strange, hairless dog walking on its hind legs. Farmers would find their animals drained and lifeless with mysterious puncture marks.

**The Creepy Part:** It supposedly strikes at night, silently, leaving almost no tracks behind. Witnesses say just *looking* into its red eyes made them feel weak and dizzy.

---

### 🦕 3. The Loch Ness Monster ("Nessie")
**The Legend:** In a deep, dark, murky lake in Scotland — so dark that visibility underwater is only a few feet — something enormous has been spotted for nearly 1,500 years. Witnesses describe a long neck rising from the water like a prehistoric plesiosaur that somehow survived extinction. Sonar readings have detected large, unexplained objects moving beneath the surface.

**The Creepy Part:** The lake is over 750 feet deep and holds more water than all the lakes of England and Wales *combined*. Something could genuinely live down there... and you'd never see it until it wanted you to.

---

### 🦋 4. Mothman
**The Legend:** In 1966 and 1967, in the small town of Point Pleasant, West Virginia, dozens of trustworthy people — doctors, firefighters, a sheriff's deputy — reported seeing a seven-foot-tall winged figure with huge, glowing red eyes. Some claimed it chased their cars at over 100 miles per hour. Then, in December 1967, the town's Silver Bridge collapsed, killing 46 people. After the tragedy, Mothman was never seen in Point Pleasant again.

**The Creepy Part:** Some believe Mothman wasn't *causing* the disaster — he was *warning* people it was coming. And whenever a new Mothman sighting is reported anywhere in the world... some say disaster follows soon after.

---

**Teacher's bonus question to leave them thinking:** *"If these creatures don't exist, why have so many honest people — from sheriffs to scientists — reported seeing them?"* 👀
